entries.9776a1223346da52df8988d9dcca298dccb8d57b: <div sID="gen15659" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Isa.9" sID="Isa.9"/> <div eID="gen15659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15660" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15661" type="x-p"/> The prophet in this chapter (according to the directions given him, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10-Isa.3.11">ch. iii. 10, 11</reference>) saith to the righteous, It shall be well with thee, but Woe to the wicked, it shall be ill with him. Here are, I. Gracious promises to those that adhere to the law and to the testimony; while those that seek to familiar spirits shall be driven into darkness and dimness, they shall see a great light, relief in the midst of their distresses, typical of gospel grace. 1. In the doctrine of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.4-Isa.9.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. 3. His government and dominion as Immanuel, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6-Isa.9.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. II. Dreadful threatenings against the people of Israel, who had revolted from and were enemies to the house of David, that they should be brought to utter ruin, that their pride should bring them down (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.8-Isa.9.10">ver. 8-10</reference>), that their neighbours should make a prey of them (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.11-Isa.9.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>), that, for their impenitence and hypocrisy, all their ornaments and supports should be cut off (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13-Isa.9.17">ver. 13-17</reference>), and that by the wrath of God against them, and their wrath one against another, they should be brought to utter ruin, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.18-Isa.9.21">ver. 18-21</reference>. And this is typical of the final destruction of all the enemies of the Son of David and his kingdom.
entries.18f25b496a3fa942cb7549c661cf49b33239d8b8: <div eID="gen15661" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15660" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgment and Mercy; The Promise of Gospel Grace; The Promise of Messiah; The Titles of Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  740.)</title> <div sID="gen15662" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Nevertheless the dimness <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> such as <hi type="italic">was</hi> in her vexation, when at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict <hi type="italic">her by</hi> the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations. <hi type="super">2</hi> The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined. <hi type="super">3</hi> Thou hast multiplied the nation, <hi type="italic">and</hi> not increased the joy: they joy before thee according to the joy in harvest, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as <hi type="italic">men</hi> rejoice when they divide the spoil. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thou hast broken the yoke of his burden, and the staff of his shoulder, the rod of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian. <hi type="super">5</hi> For every battle of the warrior <hi type="italic">is</hi> with confused noise, and garments rolled in blood; but <hi type="italic">this</hi> shall be with burning <hi type="italic">and</hi> fuel of fire. <hi type="super">6</hi> For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. <hi type="super">7</hi> Of the increase of <hi type="italic">his</hi> government and peace <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever. The zeal of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts will perform this. <div eID="gen15662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15663" type="x-p"/> The first words of this chapter plainly refer to the close of the foregoing chapter, where every thing looked black and melancholy: <hi type="italic">Behold, trouble, and darkness, and dimness</hi>—very bad, yet not so bad but that <hi type="italic">to the upright there shall arise light in the darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">Ps. cxii. 4</reference>) and <hi type="italic">at evening time it shall be light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.14.7">Zech. xiv. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Nevertheless it shall not be such dimness</hi> (either not such for kind or not such for degree) as sometimes there has been. Note, In the worst of times God's people have a <hi type="italic">nevertheless</hi> to comfort themselves with, something to allay and balance their troubles; they are persecuted, but not forsaken (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">2 Cor. iv. 9</reference>), sorrowful yet always rejoicing, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2 Cor. vi. 10</reference>. And it is matter of comfort to us, when things are at the darkest, that he who <hi type="italic">forms the light and creates the darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.7">ch. xlv. 7</reference>) has appointed to both their bounds and set the one over against the other, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.4">Gen. iv. 4</reference>. He can say, "Hitherto the dimness shall go, so long it shall last, and no further, no longer." <div eID="gen15663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15664" type="x-p"/> I. Three things are here promised, and they all point ultimately at the grace of the gospel, which the saints then were to comfort themselves with the hopes of in every cloudy and dark day, as we now are to comfort ourselves in time of trouble with the hopes of Christ's second coming, though that be now, as his first coming then was, a thing at a great distance. The mercy likewise which God has in store for his church in the latter days may be a support to those that are mourning with her for her present calamities. We have here the promise, <div eID="gen15664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15665" type="x-p"/> 1. Of a glorious light, which shall so qualify, and by degrees dispel, the dimness, that it shall not be as it sometimes has been: <hi type="italic">Not such as was in her vexation;</hi> there shall not be such dark times as were formerly, <hi type="italic">when at first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and Naphtali</hi> (which lay remote and most exposed to the inroads of the neighbouring enemies), <hi type="italic">and afterwards he more grievously afflicted the land by the way of the sea and beyond Jordan</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">v. 1</reference>), referring probably to those days when <hi type="italic">God began to cut Israel short</hi> and to <hi type="italic">smite them in all their coasts,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32">2 Kings x. 32</reference>. Note, God tries what less judgments will do with a people before he brings greater; but if a light affliction do not do its work with us, to humble and reform us, we must expect to be afflicted more grievously; for when God judges he will overcome. Well, those were dark times with the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, and there was <hi type="italic">dimness of anguish in Galilee of the Gentiles,</hi> both in respect of ignorance (they did not speak according <hi type="italic">to the law and the testimony,</hi> and then there was <hi type="italic">no light in them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.20">ch. viii. 20</reference>) and in respect of trouble, and the desperate posture of their outward affairs; we have both together, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2 Chron. xv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Israel has been without the true God and a teaching priest, and in those times there was no peace.</hi> But the dimness threatened (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.22">ch. viii. 22</reference>) shall not prevail to such a degree; for (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">v. 2</reference>) <hi type="italic">the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.</hi> (1.) At this time when the prophet lived, there were many prophets in Judah and Israel, whose prophecies were a great light both for direction and comfort to the people of God, who adhered to the law and the testimony. Besides the written word, they had prophecy; there were those that had shown them how long (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Ps. lxxiv. 9</reference>), which was a great satisfaction to them, when in respect of their outward troubles they <hi type="italic">sat in darkness, and dwelt in the land of the shadow of death.</hi> (2.) This was to have its full accomplishment when our Lord Jesus began to appear as a prophet, and to preach the gospel in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, and in Galilee of the Gentiles. And the Old-Testament prophets, as they were witnesses to him, so they were types of him. When he came and dwelt in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, then this prophecy is said to have been fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.13-Matt.4.16">Matt. iv. 13-16</reference>. Note, [1.] Those that want the gospel walk in darkness, and know not what they do nor whither they go; and they dwell in the land of the shadow of death, in thick darkness, and in the utmost danger. [2.] When the gospel comes to any place, to any soul, light comes, a great light, a shining light, which will shine more and more. It should be welcome to us, as light is to those that sit in darkness, and we should readily entertain it, both because if is of such sovereign use to us and because it brings its own evidence with it. Truly this light is sweet. <div eID="gen15665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15666" type="x-p"/> 2. Of a glorious increase, and a universal joy arising from it, (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">v. 3</reference>) "<hi type="italic">Thou,</hi> O God! <hi type="italic">hast multiplied the nation,</hi> the Jewish nation which thou hast mercy in store for; though it has been diminished by one sore judgment after another, yet now thou hast begun to multiply it again." The numbers of a nation are its strength and wealth if the numerous be industrious; and it is God that increases nations, <reference osisRef="Job.12.23">Job xii. 23</reference>. Yet it follows, "<hi type="italic">Thou hast not increased the joy</hi>—the carnal joy and mirth, and those things that are commonly the matter and occasion thereof. But, notwithstanding that, <hi type="italic">they joy before thee;</hi> there is a great deal of serious spiritual joy among them, joy in the presence of God, with an eye to him." This is very applicable to the times of gospel light, spoken of <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">v. 2</reference>. Then God multiplied the nation, the gospel Israel. "And to him" (so the Masorites read it) "thou hast magnified the joy, to every one that receives the light." The following words favour this reading: <hi type="italic">"They joy before thee;</hi> they come before thee in holy ordinances with great joy'; their mirth is not like that of Israel under their vines and fig-trees (thou hast not increased that joy), but it is in the favour of God and in the tokens of his grace." Note, The gospel, when it comes in its light and power, brings joy along with it, and those who receive it aright do therein rejoice, yea, and will rejoice; therefore the conversion of the nations is prophesied of by this (<reference osisRef="Ps.67.4">Ps. lxvii. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let the nations be glad, and sin for joy.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Ps. xcvi. 11</reference>. (1.) It is holy joy: <hi type="italic">They joy before thee;</hi> they rejoice in spirit (as Christ did, <reference osisRef="Luke.10.21">Luke x. 21</reference>), and that is before God. In the eye of the world they are always as sorrowful, and yet, in God's sight, <hi type="italic">always rejoicing,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2 Cor. vi. 10</reference>. (2.) It is great joy; it is <hi type="italic">according to the joy in harvest,</hi> when those who sowed in tears, and have with long patience waited for the precious fruits of the earth, reap in joy; and as in war men rejoice when, after a hazardous battle, <hi type="italic">they divide the spoil.</hi> The gospel brings with it plenty and victory; but those that would have the joy of it must expect to go through a hard work, as the husbandman before he has the joy of harvest, and a hard conflict, as the soldier before he has the joy of dividing the spoil; but the joy, when it comes, will be an abundant recompence for the toil. See <reference osisRef="Acts.8.8">Acts viii. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.39">39</reference>. <div eID="gen15666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15667" type="x-p"/> 3. Of a glorious liberty and enlargement (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.4-Isa.9.5">v. 4, 5</reference>): "They shall rejoice before thee, and with good reason, <hi type="italic">for thou hast broken the yoke of his burden,</hi> and made him easy, for he shall no longer be in servitude; and thou hast broken <hi type="italic">the staff of his shoulder and the rod of his oppressor,</hi> that rod of the wicked which rested long on the lot of the righteous," as the Midianites' yoke was broken from off the neck of Israel by the agency of Gideon. If God makes former deliverances his patterns in working for us, we ought to make them our encouragements to hope in him and to seek to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.9">Ps. lxxxiii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Do unto them as to the Midianites.</hi> What temporal deliverance this refers to is not clear, probably the preventing of Sennacherib from making himself master of Jerusalem, which was done, <hi type="italic">as in the day of Midian,</hi> by the immediate hand of God; and, whereas other battles were usually won with a great deal of noise and by the expense of much blood, this shall be done silently and without noise. <hi type="italic">Under his glory God shall kindle a burning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">ch. x. 16</reference>); a <hi type="italic">fire not blown shall consume him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.20.26">Job xx. 26</reference>. But doubtless it looks further, to the blessed fruits and effects of that great light which should visit those that sat in darkness; it would bring liberty along with it, <hi type="italic">deliverance to the captives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Luke iv. 18</reference>. (1.) The design of the gospel, and the grace of it, is to break the yoke of sin and Satan, to remove the burden of guilt and corruption, and to free us from the rod of those oppressors, that we might be brought into the glorious liberty of the children of God. Christ broke the yoke of the ceremonial law (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.10">Acts xv. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.1">Gal. v. 1</reference>), and delivered us <hi type="italic">out of the hand of our enemies,</hi> that we might <hi type="italic">serve him without fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">Luke i. 74, 75</reference>. (2.) This is done by the Spirit working like fire (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Matt. iii. 11</reference>), not as the battle of the warrior is fought, with confused noise; no, the weapons of our warfare are not carnal; but it is done with the Spirit of judgment and the Spirit of burning, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.4">ch. iv. 4</reference>. It is done <hi type="italic">as in the day of Midian,</hi> by a work of God upon the hearts of men. Christ is our Gideon; it is his sword that doeth wonders. <div eID="gen15667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15668" type="x-p"/> II. But who, where, is he that shall undertake and accomplish these great things for the church? The prophet tells us (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6-Isa.9.7">v. 6, 7</reference>) they shall be done by the Messiah, <hi type="italic">Immanuel,</hi> that son of a virgin whose birth he had foretold (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">ch. vii. 14</reference>), and now speaks of, in the prophetic style, as a thing already done: the <hi type="italic">child is born,</hi> not only because it was as certain, and he was as certain of it as if it had been done already, but because the church before his incarnation reaped great benefit and advantage by his undertaking in virtue of that first promise concerning the <hi type="italic">seed of the woman,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>. As he was the Lamb slain, so he was the child born, <hi type="italic">from the foundation of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Rev. xiii. 8</reference>. All the great things that God did for the Old-Testament church were done by him as the eternal Word, and for his sake as the Mediator. He was the Anointed, to whom God had respect (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.9">Ps. lxxxiv. 9</reference>), and it was for the Lord's sake, for the Lord Christ's sake, that God caused his face to shine upon his sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.17">Dan. ix. 17</reference>. The Jewish nation, and particularly the house of David, were preserved many a time from imminent ruin only because that blessing was in them. What greater security therefore could be given to the church of God then that it should be preserved, and be the special care of the divine Providence, than this, that God had so great a mercy in reserve for it? The Chaldee paraphrast understands it of the man that shall endure for ever, even Christ. And it is an illustrious prophecy of him and of his kingdom, which doubtless those that waited for the consolation of Israel built much upon, often turned to, and read with pleasure. <div eID="gen15668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15669" type="x-p"/> 1. See him in his humiliation. The same that is <hi type="italic">the mighty God</hi> is <hi type="italic">a child born;</hi> the ancient of days becomes an infant of a span long; the <hi type="italic">everlasting Father</hi> is <hi type="italic">a Son given.</hi> Such was his condescension in taking our nature upon him; thus did he humble and empty himself, to exalt and fill us. He is born into our world. <hi type="italic">The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.</hi> He is given, freely given, to be all that to us which our case, in our fallen state, calls for. God so loved the world that he gave him. He is born <hi type="italic">to us,</hi> he is given to us, us men, and not to the angels that sinned. It is spoken with an air of triumph, and the angel seems to refer to these words in the notice he gives to the shepherds of the Messiah's having come (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.11">Luke ii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Unto you is born, this day, a Saviour.</hi> Note, Christ's being born and given to us is the great foundation of our hopes, and fountain of our joys, in times of greatest grief and fear. <div eID="gen15669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15670" type="x-p"/> 2. See him in his exaltation. This child, this son, this Son of God, this Son of man, that is given to us, is in a capacity to do us a great deal of kindness; for he is invested with the highest honour and power, so that we cannot but be happy if he be our friend. <div eID="gen15670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15671" type="x-p"/> (1.) See the dignity he is advanced to, and the name he has above every name. He shall be called (and therefore we are sure he is and shall be) <hi type="italic">Wonderful, Counsellor, &c.</hi> His people shall know him and worship him by these names; and, as one that fully answers them, they shall submit to him and depend upon him. [1.] He is <hi type="italic">wonderful, counsellor.</hi> Justly is he called <hi type="italic">wonderful,</hi> for he is both God and man. His love is the wonder of angels and glorified saints; in his birth, life, death, resurrection, and ascension, he was wonderful. A constant series of wonders attended him, and, without controversy, great was the mystery of godliness concerning him. He is the <hi type="italic">counsellor,</hi> for he was intimately acquainted with the counsels of God from eternity, and he gives counsel to the children of men, in which he consults our welfare. It is by him that God has <hi type="italic">given us counsel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">Ps. xvi. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Rev. iii. 18</reference>. He is the wisdom of the Father, and is made of God to us wisdom. Some join these together: He is the wonderful counsellor, a wonder or miracle of a counsellor; in this, as in other things, he has the pre-eminence; none teaches like him. [2.] He is <hi type="italic">the mighty God—God, the mighty One.</hi> As he has wisdom, so he has strength, to go through with his undertaking: he is able to save to the utmost; and such is the work of the Mediator that no less a power than that of the mighty God could accomplish it. [3.] He is <hi type="italic">the everlasting Father,</hi> or <hi type="italic">the Father of eternity;</hi> he is God, one with the Father, who is from everlasting to everlasting. He is the author of everlasting life and happiness to them, and so is the Father of a blessed eternity to them. He is <hi type="italic">the Father of the world to come</hi> (so the LXX. reads it), the father of the gospel-state, which is put in subjection to him, not to the angels, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.5">Heb. ii. 5</reference>. He was, from eternity, Father of the great work of redemption: his heart was upon it; it was the product of his wisdom as <hi type="italic">the counsellor,</hi> of his love as <hi type="italic">the everlasting Father.</hi> [4.] He is <hi type="italic">the prince of peace.</hi> As a King, he preserves the peace, commands peace, nay, he creates peace, in his kingdom. He is our peace, and it is his peace that both keeps the hearts of his people and rules in them. He is not only a peaceable prince, and his reign peaceable, but he is the author and giver of all good, all that peace which is the present and future bliss of his subjects. <div eID="gen15671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15672" type="x-p"/> (2.) See the dominion he is advanced to, and the throne he has above every throne (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The government shall be upon his shoulder</hi>—his only. He shall not only wear the badge of it upon his shoulder (the <hi type="italic">key of the house of David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">ch. xxii. 22</reference>), but he shall bear the burden of it. The Father shall devolve it upon him, so that he shall have an incontestable right to govern; and he shall undertake it, so that no doubt can be made of his governing well, for he shall set his shoulder to it, and will never complain, as Moses did, of his being overcharged. <hi type="italic">I am not able to bear all this people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.11.11">Num. xi. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.11.14">14</reference>. Glorious things are here spoken of Christ's government, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">v. 7</reference>. [1.] That it shall be an increasing government. It shall be multiplied; the bounds of his kingdom shall be more and more enlarged, and many shall be added to it daily. The lustre of it shall increase, and it shall shine more and more brightly in the world. The monarchies of the earth were each less illustrious than the other, so that what began in gold ended in iron and clay, and every monarchy dwindled by degrees; but the kingdom of Christ is a growing kingdom, and will come to perfection at last. [2.] That it shall be a peaceable government, agreeable to his character as the prince of peace. He shall rule by love, shall rule in men's hearts; so that wherever his government is there shall be peace, and as his government increases the peace shall increase. The more we are subject to Christ the more easy and safe we are. [3.] That it shall be a rightful government. He that is the Son of David shall reign upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, which he is entitled to. <hi type="italic">God shall give him the throne of his father David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32-Luke.1.33">Luke i. 32, 33</reference>. The gospel church, in which Jew and Gentile are incorporated, is the holy hill of Zion, on which Christ reigns, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>. [4.] That it shall be administered with prudence and equity, and so as to answer the great end of government, which is the establishment of the kingdom: <hi type="italic">He shall order it, and settle it, with justice and judgment.</hi> Every thing is, and shall be, well managed, in the kingdom of Christ, and none of his subjects shall ever have cause to complain. [5.] That it shall be an everlasting kingdom: <hi type="italic">There shall be no end of the increase of his government</hi> (it shall be still growing), no end of the increase of the peace of it, for the happiness of the subjects of this kingdom shall last to eternity and perhaps shall be progressive <hi type="italic">in infinitum—for ever.</hi> He shall reign <hi type="italic">henceforth even for ever;</hi> not only throughout all generations of time, but, even when the kingdom shall be delivered up to God even the Father, the glory both of the Redeemer and the redeemed shall continue eternally. [6.] That God himself has undertaken to bring all this about: "<hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts,</hi> who has all power in his hand and all creatures at his beck, <hi type="italic">shall perform this,</hi> shall preserve the throne of David till this prince of peace is settled in it; his <hi type="italic">zeal</hi> shall do it, his jealousy for his own honour, and the truth of his promise, and the good of his church." Note, The heart of God is much upon the advancement of the kingdom of Christ among men, which is very comfortable to all those that wish well to it; <hi type="italic">the zeal of the Lord of hosts</hi> will overcome all opposition.
entries.4a4a3d7e97a0aabad5c01a2dac01e6256d52aaef: <div eID="gen15672" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings against Judah; Threatenings against Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15673" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it hath lighted upon Israel. <hi type="super">9</hi> And all the people shall know, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria, that say in the pride and stoutness of heart, <hi type="super">10</hi> The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change <hi type="italic">them into</hi> cedars. <hi type="super">11</hi> Therefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall set up the adversaries of Rezin against him, and join his enemies together; <hi type="super">12</hi> The Syrians before, and the Philistines behind; and they shall devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> stretched out still. <hi type="super">13</hi> For the people turneth not unto him that smiteth them, neither do they seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush, in one day. <hi type="super">15</hi> The ancient and honourable, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the head; and the prophet that teacheth lies, he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the tail. <hi type="super">16</hi> For the leaders of this people cause <hi type="italic">them</hi> to err; and <hi type="italic">they that are</hi> led of them <hi type="italic">are</hi> destroyed. <hi type="super">17</hi> Therefore the Lord shall have no joy in their young men, neither shall have mercy on their fatherless and widows: for every one <hi type="italic">is</hi> a hypocrite and an evil doer, and every mouth speaketh folly. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> stretched out still. <hi type="super">18</hi> For wickedness burneth as the fire: it shall devour the briers and thorns, and shall kindle in the thickets of the forest, and they shall mount up <hi type="italic">like</hi> the lifting up of smoke. <hi type="super">19</hi> Through the wrath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts is the land darkened, and the people shall be as the fuel of the fire: no man shall spare his brother. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he shall snatch on the right hand, and be hungry; and he shall eat on the left hand, and they shall not be satisfied: they shall eat every man the flesh of his own arm: <hi type="super">21</hi> Manasseh, Ephraim; and Ephraim, Manasseh: <hi type="italic">and</hi> they together <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> against Judah. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> stretched out still. <div eID="gen15673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15674" type="x-p"/> Here are terrible threatenings, which are directed primarily against Israel, the kingdom of the ten tribes, Ephraim and Samaria, the ruin of which is here foretold, with all the woeful confusions that were the prefaces to that ruin, all which came to pass within a few years after; but they look further, to all the enemies of the throne and kingdom of Christ the Son of David, and read the doom of all the nations that forget God, and will not have Christ to reign over them. Observe, <div eID="gen15674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15675" type="x-p"/> I. The preface to this prediction (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord sent a word into Jacob,</hi> sent it by his servants the prophets. He warns before he wounds. He sent notice what he would do, that they might meet him in the way of his judgments; but they would not take the hint, took no care to turn away his wrath, and so it lighted upon Israel; for no word of God shall fall to the ground. It fell upon them as a storm of rain and hail from on high, which they could not avoid: <hi type="italic">It has lighted upon them,</hi> that is, it is as sure to come as if come already, and all the people shall know by feeling it what they would not know by hearing of it. Those that are willingly ignorant of the wrath of God revealed from heaven against sin and sinners shall be made to know it. <div eID="gen15675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15676" type="x-p"/> II. The sins charged upon the people of Israel, which provoked God to bring these judgments upon them. 1. Their insolent defiance of the justice of God, thinking themselves a match for him: "They <hi type="italic">say, in the pride and stoutness of their heart,</hi> Let God himself do his worst; we will hold our own, and make our part good with him. If he ruin our houses, we will repair them, and make them stronger and finer than they were before. Our landlord shall not turn us out of doors, though we pay him no rent, but we will keep in possession. If the houses that were built of bricks be demolished in the war, we will rebuild them with hewn stones, that shall not so easily be thrown down. If the enemy cut down the sycamores, we will plant cedars in the room of them. We will make a hand of God's judgments, gain by them, and so outbrave them." Note, Those are ripening apace for ruin whose hearts are unhumbled under humbling providences; for God will walk contrary to those who thus walk contrary to him and provoke him to jealousy, as if they were stronger than he. 2. Their incorrigibleness under all the rebukes of Providence hitherto (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">v. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">The people turn not unto him that smiteth them</hi> (they are not wrought upon to reform their lives, to forsake their sins, and to return to their duty), <hi type="italic">neither do they seek the Lord of hosts;</hi> either they are atheists, and have no religion, or idolaters, and seek to those gods that are the creatures of their own fancy and the works of their own hands. Note, That which God designs, in smiting us, is to turn us to himself and to set us a seeking him; and, if this point be not gained by less judgments, greater may be expected. God smites that he may not kill. 3. Their general corruption of manners and abounding profaneness. (1.) Those that should have reformed them helped to debauch them (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The leaders of this people</hi> mislead them, and <hi type="italic">cause them to err,</hi> by conniving at their wickedness and countenancing wicked people, and by setting them bad examples; and then no wonder if those that are led of them be deceived and so destroyed. But it is ill with a people when their physicians are their worst disease. "<hi type="italic">Those that bless this people,</hi> or <hi type="italic">call them blessed</hi> (so the margin reads it), that flatter them, and soothe them in their wickedness, and cry <hi type="italic">Peace, peace, to them,</hi> cause them to err; and those <hi type="italic">that are called blessed of them are swallowed up</hi> ere they are aware." We have reason to be afraid of those that speak well of us when we do ill; see <reference osisRef="Prov.24.24">Prov. xxiv. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.29.5">xxix. 5</reference>. (2.) Wickedness was universal, and all were infected with it (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">Every one is a hypocrite and an evil doer.</hi> If there be any that are good, they do not, they dare not appear, for every mouth speaks folly and villany; every one is profane towards God (so the word properly signifies) and an evil doer towards man. These two commonly go together: those that fear not God regard not man; and then every mouth speaks folly, falsehood, and reproach, both against God and man; for <hi type="italic">out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.</hi> <div eID="gen15676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15677" type="x-p"/> III. The judgments threatened against them for this wickedness of theirs; let them not think to go unpunished. <div eID="gen15677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15678" type="x-p"/> 1. In general, hereby they exposed themselves to the wrath of God, which should both devour as fire and darken as smoke. (1.) It should devour as fire (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wickedness shall burn as the fire;</hi> the displeasure of God, incurred by sin, shall consume the sinners, who have made themselves as briers and thorns before it, and as the thickets of the forest, combustible matter, which the wrath of the Lord of hosts, the mighty God, will go through and burn together. (2.) It should darken as smoke. The briers and thorns, when the fire consumes them, shall <hi type="italic">mount up like the lifting up of smoke,</hi> so that the whole land shall be darkened by it; they shall be in trouble, and see no way out (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The people shall be as the fuel of the fire.</hi> God's wrath fastens upon none but those that make themselves fuel for it, and then they mount up as the smoke of sacrifices, being made victims to divine justice. <div eID="gen15678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15679" type="x-p"/> 2. God would arm the neighbouring powers against them, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.11-Isa.9.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. At this time the kingdom of Israel was in league with that of Syria against Judah; but the Assyrians, who were adversaries to the Syrians, when they had conquered them should invade Israel, and God would stir them up to do it, and join the enemies of Israel together in alliance against them, who yet had particular ends of their own to serve and were not aware of God's hand in their alliance. Note, When enemies are set up, and joined in confederacy against a people, God's hand must be acknowledged in it. Note further, Those that partake with each other in sin, as Syria and Israel in invading Judah, must expect to share in the punishment of sin. Nay, the Syrians themselves, whom they were now in league with, should be a scourge to them (for it is no unusual thing for those to fall out that have been united in sin), one attacking them in the front and the other flanking them or falling upon their rear; so that they should be surrounded with enemies on all sides, who should <hi type="italic">devour them with open mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">v. 12</reference>. The Philistines were not now looked upon as formidable enemies, and the Syrians were looked upon as firm friends; and yet these shall devour Israel. When men's ways displease the Lord he makes even their friends to be at war with them. <div eID="gen15679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15680" type="x-p"/> 3. God would take from the midst of them those they confided in and promised themselves help from, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.14-Isa.9.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. Because the people seek not God, those they seek to and depend upon shall stand them in no stead. <hi type="italic">The Lord will cut off head and tail, branch and rush,</hi> which is explained in the <reference osisRef="Isa.9.15">next verse</reference>. (1.) Their magistrates, who were honourable by birth and office and were the ancients of the people, these were <hi type="italic">the head,</hi> these were the branch which they promised themselves spirit and fruit from; but because these caused them to err they should be cut off, and their dignity and power should be no protection to them when the abuse of that dignity and power was the great provocation: and it was a judgment upon the people to have their princes cut off, though they were not such as they should have been. (2.) Their prophets, their false prophets, were <hi type="italic">the tail</hi> and the <hi type="italic">rush,</hi> the most despicable of all. A wicked minister is the worst of all. A wicked minister is the worst of men. <hi type="italic">Corruptio optimi est pessima—The best things become when corrupted the worst.</hi> The blind led the blind, and so both fell into the ditch; and the blind leaders fell first and fell undermost. <div eID="gen15680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15681" type="x-p"/> 4. That the desolation should be as general as the corruption had been, and none should escape it, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.17">v. 17</reference>. (1.) Not those that were the objects of complacency. None shall be spared for love: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall have no joy in their young men,</hi> that were in the flower of their youth; nor will he say, <hi type="italic">Deal gently with the young men for my sake;</hi> no, "Let them fall with the rest, and with them let the seed of the next generation perish." (2.) Not those that were the objects of compassion. None shall be spared for pity: He <hi type="italic">shall not have mercy on their fatherless and widows,</hi> though he is, in a particular manner, the patron and protector of such. They had corrupted their way like all the rest; and, if the poverty and helplessness of their state was not an argument with them to keep them from sin, they could not expect it should be an argument with God to protect them from judgments. <div eID="gen15681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15682" type="x-p"/> 5. That they should pull one another to pieces, that every one should help forward the common ruin, and they should be cannibals to themselves and one to another: <hi type="italic">No man shall spare his brother,</hi> if he come in the way of his ambition of covetousness, or if he have any colour to be revenged on him; and how can they expect God should spare them when they show no compassion one to another? Men's passion and cruelty one against another provoke God to be angry with them all and are an evidence that he is so. Civil wars soon bring a kingdom to desolation. Such there were in Israel, when, <hi type="italic">for the transgression of the land, many were the princes thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.2">Prov. xxviii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen15682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15683" type="x-p"/> (1.) In these intestine broils, men <hi type="italic">snatched on the right hand, and yet were hungry</hi> still, and did eat the <hi type="italic">flesh of their own arms,</hi> preyed upon themselves for hunger or upon their nearest relations that were as their own flesh, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.20">v. 20</reference>. This bespeaks, [1.] Great famine and scarcity; when men had pulled all they could to them it was so little that they were still hungry, at least God did not bless it to them, so that <hi type="italic">they eat and have not enough,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hag.1.6">Hag. i. 6</reference>. [2.] Great rapine and plunder. <hi type="italic">Jusque datum sceleri—iniquity is established by law.</hi> The hedge of property, which is a hedge of protection to men's estates, shall be plucked up, and every man shall think all that his own which he can lay his hands on (<hi type="italic">vivitur ex rapto, non hospes ab hospite tutus—they live on the spoil, and the rites of hospitality are all violated</hi>); and yet, when men thus catch at that which is none of their own, they are not satisfied. Covetous desires are insatiable, and this curse is entailed on that which is ill got, that it will never do well. <div eID="gen15683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15684" type="x-p"/> (2.) These intestine broils should be not only among particular persons and private families, but among the tribes (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Manasseh shall devour Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh,</hi> though they be combined against Judah. Those that could unite against Judah could not unite with one another; but that sinful confederacy of theirs against their neighbour <hi type="italic">that dwelt securely by them</hi> was justly punished by this separation of them one from another. Or Judah, having sinned like Manasseh and Ephraim, shall not only suffer with them, but suffer by them. Note, Mutual enmity and animosity among the tribes of God's Israel is a sin that ripens them for ruin, and a sad symptom of ruin hastening on apace. If Ephraim be against Manasseh, and Manasseh against Ephraim, and both against Judah, they will all soon become a very easy prey to the common enemy. <div eID="gen15684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15685" type="x-p"/> 6. That, though they should be followed with all these judgments, yet God would not let fall his controversy with them. It is the heavy burden of this song (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">v. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.17">17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.21">21</reference>): <hi type="italic">For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still,</hi> that is, (1.) They do nothing to turn away his anger; they do not repent and reform, do not humble themselves and pray, none stand in the gap, none answer God's calls nor comply with the designs of his providences, but they are hardened and secure. (2.) His anger therefore continues to burn against them and <hi type="italic">his hand is stretched out still.</hi> The reason why the judgments of God are prolonged is because the point is not gained, sinners are not brought to repentance by them. <hi type="italic">The people turn not to him that smites them,</hi> and therefore he continues to smite them; for when God judges he will overcome, and the proudest stoutest sinner shall either bend or break.  <chapter eID="Isa.9"/> <div eID="gen15685" type="x-p"/>

entries.64113caa5318b9f4fa57332c0151f2aee9504f19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8473"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.9.1-Isa.9.7">Is 9:1-7</reference>. Continuation of the Prophecy in the Eighth Chapter.</title> <div sID="gen13708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8473"/><hi type="bold">1. Nevertheless, &c.--</hi>rather, "For darkness shall not (continually) be on it (that is, the land) on which there is (now) distress" [Hengstenberg and Maurer]. The "for" refers, not to the words immediately preceding, but to the consolations in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Is 8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.17">10, 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">18</reference>. Do not despair, for, &c.<div eID="gen13708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when at the first, &c.--</hi>rather, "as the former time has brought contempt on the land of Zebulun and Naphtali (namely, the deportation of their inhabitants under Tiglath-pileser, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>, a little before the giving of this prophecy); so shall the after-coming time bring honor to the way of the sea (the district around the lake of Galilee), the land beyond (but Hengstenberg, "by the side of") Jordan (Perea, east of Jordan, belonging to Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh), the circle (but Hengstenberg, "Galilee") (that is, region) of the "Gentiles" [Maurer, Hengstenberg, &c.]. Galil in Hebrew is a "circle," "circuit," and from it came the name Galilee. North of Naphtali, inhabited by a mixed race of Jews and Gentiles of the bordering Phoenician race (<reference osisRef="Judg.1.30">Jud 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.11">1Ki 9:11</reference>). Besides the recent deportation by Tiglath-pileser, it had been sorely smitten by Ben-hadad of Syria, two hundred years before (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.20">1Ki 15:20</reference>). It was after the Assyrian deportation colonized with heathens, by Esar-haddon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.24">2Ki 17:24</reference>). Hence arose the contempt for it on the part of the southern Jews of purer blood (<reference osisRef="John.1.46">Joh 1:46</reference>; 7:52). The same region which was so darkened once, shall be among the first to receive Messiah's light (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.13">Mt 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.16">15, 16</reference>). It was in despised Galilee that He first and most publicly exercised His ministry; from it were most of His apostles. Foretold in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.18">De 33:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.7">Ac 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">Psa 68:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">28</reference>, Jerusalem, the theocratic capital, might readily have known Messiah; to compensate less favored Galilee, He ministered mostly there; Galilee's very debasement made it feel its need of a Saviour, a feeling not known to the self-righteous Jews (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Mt 9:13</reference>). It was appropriate, too, that He who was both "the Light to lighten the Gentiles, and the Glory of His people Israel," should minister chiefly on the border land of Israel, near the Gentiles. <div eID="gen13709" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b992e664766ecc1d86f0634acf9fd13de621039: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8474"/><div sID="gen13710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8474"/><hi type="bold">2. the people--</hi>the whole nation, Judah and Israel.<div eID="gen13710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow of death--</hi>the darkest misery of captivity. <div eID="gen13711" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff4256d8be24e17854531ac9c32c20013efc55e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8475"/><div sID="gen13712" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8475"/><hi type="bold">3. multiplied ... nation--</hi>primarily, the rapid increase of Israelites after the return from Babylon; more fully and exhaustively the rapid spread of Christianity at first.<div eID="gen13712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not increased the joy--</hi>By a slight change in the Hebrew, its (joy) is substituted by some for not, because "not increased the joy" seems opposite to what immediately follows, "the joy," &c. Hengstenberg, retains not thus: "Whose joy thou hadst not increased," (that is, hadst diminished). Others, "Hast thou not increased the joy?" The very difficulty of the reading, not, makes it less likely to be an interpolation. Horsley best explains it: The prophet sees in vision a shifting scene, comprehending at one glance the history of the Christian Church to remotest times--a land dark and thinly peopled--lit up by a sudden light--filled with new inhabitants--then struggling with difficulties, and again delivered by the utter and final overthrow of their enemies. The influx of Gentile converts (represented here by "Galilee of the Gentiles") soon was to be followed by the growth of corruption, and the final rise of Antichrist, who is to be destroyed, while God's people is delivered, as in the case of Gideon's victory over Midian, not by man's prowess, but by the special interposition of God.<div eID="gen13713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before thee--</hi>a phrase taken from sacrificial feasts; the tithe of harvest was eaten before God (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.7">De 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.26">14:26</reference>).<div eID="gen13714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as men rejoice ... divide ... spoil--</hi>referring to the judgments on the enemies of the Lord and His people, which usually accompany revelations of His grace. <div eID="gen13715" type="x-p"/>
entries.8206ccedd7549c272fd9a0fa814fedc8d50a34bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8476"/><div sID="gen13716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8476"/>4. The occasion of the "joy," the deliverance not only of Ahaz and Judah from the Assyrian tribute (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.8">2Ki 16:8</reference>), and of Israel's ten tribes from the oppressor (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Ki 15:19</reference>), but of the Jewish Christian Church from its last great enemy.<div eID="gen13716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hast--</hi>the past time for the future, in prophetic vision; it expresses the certainty of the event.<div eID="gen13717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yoke of his burden--</hi>the yoke with which he was burdened.<div eID="gen13718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">staff of ... shoulder--</hi>the staff which strikes his shoulder [Maurer]; or the wood, like a yoke, on the neck of slaves, the badge of servitude [Rosenmuller].<div eID="gen13719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13720" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day of Midian--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.7.8-Judg.7.22">Jud 7:8-22</reference>). As Gideon with a handful of men conquered the hosts of Midian, so Messiah the "child" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>) shall prove to be the "Prince of peace," and the small Israel under Him shall overcome the mighty hosts of Antichrist (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2-Mic.5.5">Mi 5:2-5</reference>), containing the same contrast, and alluding also to "the Assyrian," the then enemy of the Church, as here in Isaiah, the type of the last great enemy. For further analogies between Gideon's victory and the Gospel, compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2Co 4:7</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Judg.7.22">Jud 7:22</reference>. As the "dividing of the spoil" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Is 9:3</reference>) was followed by that which was "not joy," the making of the idolatrous ephod (<reference osisRef="Judg.8.24-Judg.8.27">Jud 8:24-27</reference>), so the gospel victory was soon followed by apostasy at the first, and shall be so again after the millennial overthrow of Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.3">Re 20:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.7-Rev.20.9">7-9</reference>), previous to Satan's last doom (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.10">Re 20:10</reference>). <div eID="gen13720" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc9c2d3af47fc35162f079d121a21f547838e276: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8477"/><div sID="gen13721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8477"/><hi type="bold">5. every battle, &c.--</hi>rather, "every greave of (the warrior who is) armed with greaves in the din of battle, and the martial garment (or cloak, called by the Latins sagum) rolled in blood, shall be for burning, (and) fuel for fire" [Maurer]. All warlike accoutrements shall be destroyed, as no longer required in the new era of peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Is 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.6">11:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.46.9">Psa 46:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.9">Eze 39:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.5">Mi 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">10</reference>). Compare Mal 4:1, as to the previous burning up of the wicked. <div eID="gen13721" type="x-p"/>
entries.21dcd04fd797116d304482684e34c1f540a13155: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8478"/><div sID="gen13722" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8478"/><hi type="bold">6. For--</hi>the ground of these great expectations,<div eID="gen13722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto us--</hi>for the benefit of the Jews first, and then the Gentiles (compare "unto you," <reference osisRef="Luke.2.11">Lu 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen13723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son ... given--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Psa 2:7</reference>). God's gratuitous gift, on which man had no claim (<reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.23">Ro 6:23</reference>).<div eID="gen13724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">government ... upon ... shoulder--</hi>The ensign of office used to be worn on the shoulder, in token of sustaining the government (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">Is 22:22</reference>). Here the government on Messiah's shoulder is in marked antithesis to the "yoke and staff" of the oppressor on Israel's "shoulder" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Is 9:4</reference>). He shall receive the kingdom of the earth from the Father, to vindicate it from the misrule of those to whom it was entrusted to hold it for and under the Most High, but who sought to hold it in defiance of His right; the Father asserts His right by the Son, the "Heir of all things," who will hold it for Him (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen13725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name ... called--</hi>His essential characteristics shall be.<div eID="gen13726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Wonderful--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.8.18">Is 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.13.18">Jud 13:18</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen13727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Counsellor--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">Psa 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">1Co 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen13728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">Is 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.8">Psa 24:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>) Horsley translates: "God the mighty man." "Unto us ... God" is equivalent to "Immanuel" (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Is 7:14</reference>).<div eID="gen13729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting Father--</hi>This marks Him as "Wonderful," that He is "a child," yet the "everlasting Father" (<reference osisRef="John.10.30">Joh 10:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.9">14:9</reference>). Earthly kings leave their people after a short reign; He will reign over and bless them for ever [Hengstenberg].<div eID="gen13730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Prince of Peace--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Is 9:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>; Shiloh, "The Tranquillizer"). Finally (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>). Even already He is "our peace" (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Lu 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>). <div eID="gen13731" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9eb77507278ee35fa8e0cd01bcf3788f29a9009: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8479"/><div sID="gen13732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8479"/><hi type="bold">7. Of ... increase ... no end--</hi>His princely rule shall perpetually increase and be unlimited (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>).<div eID="gen13732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">throne of David--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.25">1Ki 8:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; 132:11; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">18</reference> Eze 34:23-26; 37:<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.22">16, 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Lu 1:32</reference>, 33; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>).<div eID="gen13733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment ... justice--</hi>It is not a kingdom of mere might, and triumph of force over enemies, but of righteousness (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">Is 42:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6">Psa 45:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">7</reference>), attainable only in and by Messiah.<div eID="gen13734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">zeal, &c.--</hi>including not only Christ's hidden spiritual victory over Satan at the first coming, but the open one accompanied with "judgments" on Antichrist and every enemy at the second coming (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Is 59:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.6-Ps.9.8">Psa 9:6-8</reference>).<div eID="gen13735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13736" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8-Isa.10.4">Is 9:8-10:4</reference>. Prophecy as to the Ten Tribes.<div eID="gen13736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13737" type="x-p"/> Delivered a little later than the previous one. The ninth and tenth chapters ought to have been so divided. The present division into chapters was made by Cardinal Hugo, in A.D. 1250; and into verses, by Robert Stephens, the famous printer of Paris, in 1551. After the Assyrian invasion of Syria, that of Ephraim shall follow (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>); Is 9:8-11, 17-20, foretell the intestine discords in Israel after Hoshea had slain Pekah (A.D. 739), that is, just after the Assyrian invasions, when for seven years it was stripped of magistrates and torn into factions. There are four strophes, each setting forth Ephraim's crime and consequent punishment, and ending with the formula, "For all this His anger is not turned away," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">Is 9:12</reference>, 17, 21, and <reference osisRef="Isa.10.4">Is 10:4</reference>). <div eID="gen13737" type="x-p"/>
entries.7fb945928d09906cc4d6e629b6e6bc9f968786fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8480"/><div sID="gen13738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8480"/>8. Heading of the prophecy; (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.8-Isa.9.12">Is 9:8-12</reference>), the first strophe.<div eID="gen13738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto Jacob--</hi>against the ten tribes [Lowth].<div eID="gen13739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lighted upon--</hi>fallen from heaven by divine revelation (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.31">Da 4:31</reference>). <div eID="gen13740" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a75ddd90bcc95286555cdb91458dea9dd54b905: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8481"/><div sID="gen13741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8481"/><hi type="bold">9. know--</hi>to their cost: experimentally (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.7">Ho 9:7</reference>).<div eID="gen13741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Samaria--</hi>the capital of Ephraim (compare as to phrase, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Is 1:1</reference>). <div eID="gen13742" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca08ddb8e124b24ccc57fcc6af3ddf27c4684c40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8482"/><div sID="gen13743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8482"/><hi type="bold">10. bricks--</hi>in the East generally sun-dried, and therefore soon dissolved by rain. Granting, say the Ephraimites to the prophet's threat, that our affairs are in a ruinous state, we will restore them to more than their former magnificence. Self-confident unwillingness to see the judgments of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Is 26:11</reference>).<div eID="gen13743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hewn stones--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.17">1Ki 5:17</reference>).<div eID="gen13744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sycamores--</hi>growing abundantly on the low lands of Judea, and though useful for building on account of their antiseptic property (which induced the Egyptians to use them for the cases of their mummies), not very valuable. The cedar, on the other hand, was odorous, free from knots, durable, and precious (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.27">1Ki 10:27</reference>). "We will replace cottages with palaces." <div eID="gen13745" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1616b6ab38849428cb8ff7e54bc151727b4ac0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8483"/><div sID="gen13746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8483"/><hi type="bold">11. adversaries of Rezin--</hi>the Assyrians, who shall first attack Damascus, shall next advance "against him" (Ephraim). This is the punishment of Ephraim's pride in making light (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.10">Is 9:10</reference>) of the judgment already inflicted by God through Tiglath-pileser (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>). A second Assyrian invasion (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.7.1">Is 7:1</reference>) shall follow. The reading "princes" for "adversaries" in uncalled for.<div eID="gen13746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">join--</hi>rather, "arm"; cover with armor [Maurer].<div eID="gen13747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his--</hi>Rezin's. <div eID="gen13748" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ef9b6efdbfb1e3722c893755b93230c7b9c0ad0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8484"/><div sID="gen13749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8484"/><hi type="bold">12. Syrians--</hi>Though now allies of Ephraim, after Rezin's death they shall join the Assyrians against Ephraim. "Together," in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.11">Is 9:11</reference>, refers to this. Conquering nations often enlist in their armies the subject races (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.35.11">Jr 35:11</reference>), [Aben Ezra, Gesenius]. Horsley less probably takes "Syrians before," as the Syrians to the east, that is, not Rezin's subjects, but the Assyrians: "Aram" being the common name of Syrians and Assyrians.<div eID="gen13749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Philistines--</hi>of Palestine.<div eID="gen13750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behind--</hi>from the west: in marking the points of the compass, Orientalists face the east, which is before them: the west is behind. The right hand is the south: the left, the north.<div eID="gen13751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devour--</hi>as a ravenous beast (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.20">Is 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jr 10:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.16">30:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.9">Nu 14:9</reference>).<div eID="gen13752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For all this, &c.--</hi>The burden of each strophe. <div eID="gen13753" type="x-p"/>
entries.794f8a763c8aa63018b5af70af2f2a79d3dd721b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8485"/><div sID="gen13754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8485"/>13-17. Second strophe.<div eID="gen13754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turneth not--</hi>the design of God's chastisements; not fulfilled in their case; a new cause for punishment (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jr 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.3">5:3</reference>). <div eID="gen13755" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea13efc326a569d81d8629357b3f1725b955bcb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8490"/><div sID="gen13767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8490"/>18-21. Third strophe.<div eID="gen13767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burneth--</hi>maketh consumption, not only spreading rapidly, but also consuming like fire: sin is its own punishment.<div eID="gen13768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">briers ... thorns--</hi>emblem of the wicked; especially those of low rank (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Is 27:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forest--</hi>from the humble shrubbery the flame spreads to the vast forest; it reaches the high, as well as the low.<div eID="gen13770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mount up like ... smoke--</hi>rather. "They (the thickets of the forest) shall lift themselves proudly aloft [the Hebrew is from a Syriac root, a cock, expressing stateliness of motion, from his strutting gait, Horsley], in (in passing into) volumes of ascending smoke" [Maurer]. <div eID="gen13771" type="x-p"/>

entries.2278378c70801e92ce46dcfa13f57ce76084d619: <div eID="gen26899" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26900" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26901" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26901" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26900" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26902" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains an illustrious prophecy of the Messiah. He is represented under the glorious figure of the sun, or light, rising on a benighted world, and diffusing joy and gladness wherever he sheds his beams, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1-Isa.9.3">Isa 9:1-3</reference>. His conquests are astonishing and miraculous, as in the day of Midian; and the peace which they procure is to be permanent, as denoted by the burning of all the implements of war, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Isa 9:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Isa 9:5</reference>. The person and character of this great Deliverer are then set forth in the most magnificent terms which the language of mankind could furnish, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference>. The extent of his kingdom is declared to be universal, and the duration of it eternal, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Isa 9:7</reference>. The prophet foretells most awful calamities which were ready to fall upon the Israelites on account of their manifold impieties, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8-Isa.9.21">Isa 9:8-21</reference>. <div eID="gen26902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26903" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen26903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26904" type="x-p"/> Dimness "Accumulated darkness" - Either מנדחה menuddechah, fem. to agree with אפלה aphelah; or אפל המנדח aphel hammenuddach, alluding perhaps to the palpable Egyptian darkness, <reference osisRef="Exo.10.21">Exo 10:21</reference>. <div eID="gen26904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26905" type="x-p"/> The land of Zebulun - Zebulun, Naphtali, Manasseh, that is, the country of Galilee all round the sea of Gennesareth, were the parts that principally suffered in the first Assyrian invasion under Tiglath-pileser; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Kgs 15:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.26">1Chr 5:26</reference>. And they were the first that enjoyed the blessings of Christ's preaching the Gospel, and exhibiting his miraculous works among them. See Mede's Works, p. 101, and 457. This, which makes the twenty-third verse of chap. 8 in the Hebrew, is the first verse in chap. 9 in our authorized version. Bishop Lowth follows the division in the Hebrew.
entries.bea857fed21b14f4d7015b5865e62d5e06d34baf: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen26905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26906" type="x-p"/> And not increased the joy "Thou hast increased their joy" - Eleven MSS. of Kennicott's and six of De Ross's, two ancient, read לו lo, it, according to the Masoretical correction, instead of לא lo, not. To the same purpose the Targum and Syriac. <div eID="gen26906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26907" type="x-p"/> The joy in harvest - כשמחת בקציר kesimchath bakkatsir. For בקציר bakkatsir one MS. of Kennicott's and one of De Rossi's have קציר katsir, and another הקציר hakkatsir, "the harvest;" one of which seems to be the true, reading, as the noun preceding is in regimine.
entries.d2ab960fda27c8353f2aa62cb3d5c18ba947af6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen26907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26908" type="x-p"/> Every battle of the warrior "The greaves of the armed warrior" - שאון שאון seon soen. This word, occurring only in this place, is oaf very doubtful signification. Schindler fairly tells us that we may guess at it by the context. The Jews have explained it, by guess I believe, as signifying battle, conflict: the Vulgate renders it violenta praedatio. But it seems as if something was rather meant which was capable of becoming fuel for the fire, together with the garments mentioned in the same sentence. In Syriac the word, as a noun, signifies a shoe, or a sandal, as a learned friend suggested to me some years ago. See <reference osisRef="Luk.15.22">Luk 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.12.8">Act 12:8</reference>. I take it, therefore, to mean that part of the armor which covered the legs and feet, and I would render the two words in Latin by caliga caligati. The burning of heaps of armor, gathered from the field of battle, as an offering made to the god supposed to be the giver of victory, was a custom that prevailed among some heathen nations; and the Romans used it as an emblem of peace, which perfectly well suits with the design of the prophet in this place. A medal struck by Vespasian on finishing his wars both at home and abroad represents the goddess Peace holding an olive branch in one hand, and, with a lighted torch in the other, setting fire to a heap of armor. Virgil mentions the custom: - " - Cum primam aciem Praeneste sub ipsa <div eID="gen26908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26909" type="x-p"/> Stravi, scutorumque incendi victor acervos." <div eID="gen26909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26910" type="x-p"/> Aen. lib. viii., ver. 561. "Would heaven, (said he), my strength and youth recall, <div eID="gen26910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26911" type="x-p"/> Such as I was beneath Praeneste's wall - <div eID="gen26911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26912" type="x-p"/> Then when I made the foremost foes retire <div eID="gen26912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26913" type="x-p"/> And set whole heaps of conquered shields on fire." <div eID="gen26913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26914" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen26914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26915" type="x-p"/> See Addison on Medals, Series 2:18. And there are notices of some such practice among the Israelites, and other nations of the most early times. God promises to Joshua victory over the kings of Canaan. "To-morrow I will deliver them up all slain before Israel: thou shalt hough their horses, and burn their chariots with fire," <reference osisRef="Jos.11.6">Jos 11:6</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="Nah.2.13">Nah 2:13</reference>. And the psalmist employs this image to express complete victory, and the perfect establishment of peace: - "He maketh wars to cease, even to the end of the land: <div eID="gen26915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26916" type="x-p"/> He breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; <div eID="gen26916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26917" type="x-p"/> And burneth the chariots in the fire. - <reference osisRef="Psa.46.9">Psa 46:9</reference>. עגלות agaloth, properly plausira, impedimenta, the baggage-wagons: which however the Septuagint and Vulgate render scuta, "shields;" and the Chaldee, "round shields," to show the propriety of that sense of the word from the etymology; which, if admitted, makes the image the same with that used by the Romans. <div eID="gen26917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26918" type="x-p"/> Ezekiel, <reference osisRef="Eze.39.8-Eze.39.10">Eze 39:8-10</reference>, in his bold manner has carried this image to a degree of amplification which I think hardly any other of the Hebrew poets would have attempted. He describes the burning of the arms of the enemy, in consequence of the complete victory to be obtained by the Israelites over Gog and Magog: - "Behold, it is come to pass, and it is done, <div eID="gen26918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26919" type="x-p"/> Saith the Lord Jehovah. <div eID="gen26919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26920" type="x-p"/> This is the day of which I spoke: <div eID="gen26920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26921" type="x-p"/> And the inhabitants of the cities of Israel shall go forth. <div eID="gen26921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26922" type="x-p"/> And shall set on fire the armor, and the shield, <div eID="gen26922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26923" type="x-p"/> And the buckler, and the bow, and the arrows, <div eID="gen26923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26924" type="x-p"/> And the clubs and the lances; <div eID="gen26924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26925" type="x-p"/> And they shall set them on fire for seven years. <div eID="gen26925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26926" type="x-p"/> And they shall not bear wood from the field; <div eID="gen26926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26927" type="x-p"/> Neither shall they hew from the forest: <div eID="gen26927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26928" type="x-p"/> For of the armor shall they make their fires; <div eID="gen26928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26929" type="x-p"/> And they shall spoil their spoilers, <div eID="gen26929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26930" type="x-p"/> And they shall plunder their plunderers." <div eID="gen26930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26931" type="x-p"/> R. D. Kimchi, on this verse says this refers simply to the destruction of the Assyrians. Other battles are fought man against man, and spear against spear; and the garments are rolled in blood through the wounds given and received: but this was with burning, for the angel of the Lord smote them by night, and there was neither sword nor violent commotion, nor blood; they were food for the fire, for the angel of the Lord consumed them.
entries.525083f96c7897bf456749438506dff08abe5164: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen26931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26932" type="x-p"/> The government shall be upon his shoulder - That is, the ensign of government; the scepter, the sword, the key, or the like, which was borne upon or hung from the shoulder. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">Isa 22:22</reference>. <div eID="gen26932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26933" type="x-p"/> And his name shall be called - אל גבור El gibbor, the prevailing or conquering God. <div eID="gen26933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26934" type="x-p"/> The everlasting Father "The Father of the everlasting age" - Or אבי עד Abi ad, the Father of eternity. The Septuagint have μεγαλης βουλης Αγγελος, "the Messenger of the Great Counsel." But instead of אבי אד Abi ad, a MS. of De Rossi has אבעזר Abezer, the helping Father; evidently the corruption of some Jew, who did not like such an evidence in favor of the Christian Messiah. <div eID="gen26934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26935" type="x-p"/> Prince of Peace - שר שלום sar shalom, the Prince of prosperity, the Giver of all blessings. <div eID="gen26935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26936" type="x-p"/> A MS. of the thirteenth century in Kennicott's collection has a remarkable addition here. "He shall be a stumbling-block, המכשלה; the government is on his shoulder." This reading is nowhere else acknowledged, as far as I know.
entries.fc05a04f783975e2225ffde41787f559f80dd7b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen26936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26937" type="x-p"/> Of the increase - In the common Hebrew Bibles, and in many MSS., this word is written with the close or final למרבה ם. But in twelve of Kennicott's MSS., and twelve of De Rossi's, it is written with the open מ mem; but here it is supposed to contain mysteries, viz., that Jerusalem shall be shut up, closed, and confined, till the days of the Messiah. <div eID="gen26937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26938" type="x-p"/> This is an illustrious prophecy of the incarnation of Christ, with an enumeration of those characters in which he stands most nearly related to mankind as their Savior; and of others by which his infinite majesty and Godhead are shown. He shall appear as a child, born of a woman, born as a Jew, under the law, but not in the way of ordinary generation. He is a Son given - the human nature, in which the fullness of the Godhead was to dwell, being produced by the creative energy of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the Virgin. See <reference osisRef="Mat.1.20">Mat 1:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.1.21">Mat 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.1.23">Mat 1:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.1.25">Mat 1:25</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Luk.1.35">Luk 1:35</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Isa 7:14</reference>, and the notes on those passages. As being God manifested in the flesh, he was wonderful in his conception, birth, preaching, miracles, sufferings, death, resurrection, and ascension; wonderful in his person, and wonderful in his working. He is the Counsellor that expounds the law; shows its origin, nature, and claims; instructs, pleads for the guilty; and ever appears in the presence of God for men. He is the mighty God; God essentially and efficiently prevailing against his enemies, and destroying ours. He is the Father of eternity; the Origin of all being, and the Cause of the existence, and particularly the Father, of the spirits of all flesh. The Prince of peace - not only the Author of peace, and the Dispenser of peace, but also he that rules by peace, whose rule tends always to perfection, and produces prosperity. Of the increase of his government - this Prince has a government, for he has all power both in heaven and in earth: and his government increases, and is daily more and more extended, and will continue till all things are put under his feet. His kingdom is ordered - every act of government regulated according to wisdom and goodness; is established so securely as not to be overthrown; and administered in judgment and justice, so as to manifest his wisdom, righteousness, goodness, and truth. Reader, such is that Jesus who came into the world to save sinners!
