Trust in Him! <div eID="gen26938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26939" type="x-p"/> Isaiah 9:8-10:4 <div eID="gen26939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26940" type="x-p"/> This whole passage reduced to its proper and entire form, and healed of the dislocation which it suffers by the absurd division of the chapters, makes a distinct prophecy, and a just poem, remarkable for the regularity of its disposition and the elegance of its plan. It has no relation to the preceding or following prophecy; though the parts, violently torn asunder, have been, on the one side and the other, patched on to them. Those relate principally to the kingdom of Judah, this is addressed exclusively to the kingdom of Israel. The subject of it is a denunciation of vengeance awaiting their crimes. It is divided into four parts, each threatening the particular punishment of some grievous offense - of their pride, of their perseverance in their vices, of their impiety, and of their injustice. To which is added a general denunciation of a farther reserve of Divine wrath, contained in a distich, before used by the prophet on a like occasion, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference>, and here repeated after each part. This makes the intercalary verse of the poem; or, as we call it, the burden of the song. "Post hoc comma (cap. <reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Isa 9:4</reference>) interponitur spatium unius lineae, in Cod. 2 et 3: idemque observatur in 245. in quo nullum est spatium ad finem capitis 9." Kennicott, Var. Lect. "After this clause (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Isa 9:4</reference>) is interposed the space of one line in Cod. 2 and 3. The same is likewise observed in Cod. 245, in which no space exists at the end of chap. 9."
entries.f8a5fe1340c5906c0a6421bb959ace81b0791b0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen26940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26941" type="x-p"/> Lord "Jehovah" - For אדני Adonai, thirty MSS. of Kennicott's, and many of De Rossi's, and three editions, read יהוה Yehovah.
entries.72c5da761a58762e5b51b8f86a162aefbbc68f15: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen26941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26942" type="x-p"/> Pride and stoutness of heart "Carry themselves haughtily" - וידעו veyadeu, "and they shall know;" so ours and the Versions in general. But what is it that they shall know? The verb stands destitute of its object; and the sense is imperfect. The Chaldee is the only one, as far as I can find, that expresses it otherwise. He renders the verb in this place by ואתרברבו veithrabrabu, "they exalt themselves, or carry themselves haughtily; the same word by which he renders גבהו gabehu, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Isa 3:16</reference>. He seems, therefore, in this place to have read ויגבהו vaiyigbehu, which agrees perfectly well with what follows, and clears up the difficulty. Archbishop Secker conjectured וידברו vayedabberu, referring it to לאמר lemor, in the next verse, which shows that he was not satisfied with the present reading. Houbigant reads וירעו vaiyereu, et pravi facti sunt, they are become wicked, which is found in a MS.; but I prefer the reading of the Chaldee, which suits much better with the context. <div eID="gen26942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26943" type="x-p"/> Houbigant approves of this reading; but it is utterly unsupported by any evidence from antiquity: it is a mere mistake of ר resh for ד daleth; and I am surprised that it should be favored by Houbigant.
entries.cc7b7178b21486dc8fd3c83bb0e2b64ad523aee8: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen26943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26944" type="x-p"/> The bricks - "The eastern bricks," says Sir John Chardin, (see Harmer's Observ. I., p. 176), "are only clay well moistened with water, and mixed with straw, and dried in the sun." So that their walls are commonly no better than our mud walls; see Maundrell, p. 124. That straw was a necessary part in the composition of this sort of bricks, to make the parts of the clay adhere together, appears from Exodus 5. These bricks are properly opposed to hewn stone, so greatly superior in beauty and durableness. The sycamores, which, as Jerome on the place says, are timber of little worth, with equal propriety are opposed to the cedars. "As the grain and texture of the sycamore is remarkably coarse and spongy, it could therefore stand in no competition at all (as it is observed, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.10">Isa 9:10</reference>) with the cedar, for beauty and ornament." - Shaw, Supplement to Travels, p. 96. We meet with the same opposition of cedars to sycamores, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.27">1Kgs 10:27</reference>, where Solomon is said to have made silver as the stones, and cedars as the sycamores in the vale for abundance. By this mashal, or figurative and sententious speech, they boast that they shall easily be able to repair their present losses, suffered perhaps by the first Assyrian invasion under Tiglath-pileser; and to bring their affairs to a more flourishing condition than ever. <div eID="gen26944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26945" type="x-p"/> Some of the bricks mentioned above lie before me. They were brought from the site of ancient Babylon. The straw is visible, kneaded with the clay; they are very hard, and evidently were dried in the sun; for they are very easily dissolved in water.
entries.c2ba1f9db639a8a204de0eea247b85247ad47192: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen26945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26946" type="x-p"/> The adversaries of Rezin against him "The princes of Retsin against him" - For צרי tsarey, enemies, Houbigant, by conjecture, reads שרי sarey, princes; which is confirmed by thirty of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., (two ancient), one of my own, ancient; and nine more have צ tsaddi, upon a rasure, and therefore had probably at first שרי sarey. The princes of Retsin, the late ally of Israel, that is, the Syrians, expressly named in the next verse, shall now be excited against Israel. <div eID="gen26946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26947" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint in this place give us another variation; for רצין Retsin, they read הר ציון har tsiyon, ορος Σιων, Mount Sion, of which this may be the sense; but Jehovah shall set up the adversaries of Mount Sion against him, (i.e., against Israel), and will strengthen his enemies together; the Syrians, the Philistines, who are called the adversaries of Mount Sion. See Simonis Lex. in voce סכך sachach.
entries.cbccd4cb597dbf16ea8ed5f605e7f91c7d70cdb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen26947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26948" type="x-p"/> With open mouth "On every side" - בכל פה bechol peh, in every corner, in every part of their country, pursuing them to the remotest extremities, and the most retired parts. So the Chaldee בכל אתר bechol athar, in every place.
entries.0701ef32877332933705f2ae0d8198b43ec461f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen26948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26949" type="x-p"/> In one day - Thirteen MSS. of Kennicott and De Rossi read ביום beyond in a day; and another has a rasure in the place of the letter ב beth.
entries.edf31a5bf7eacf959be7ca80ea0ecc6a7d2faa26: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen26949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26950" type="x-p"/> The Lord "Jehovah" - For אדני Adonai, a great number of MSS. read יהוה Yehovah.
entries.1e9a76046bfaac70ade8d91b760269b63c3097d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen26950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26951" type="x-p"/> For wickedness - Wickedness rageth like a fire, destroying and laying waste the nation: but it shall be its own destruction, by bringing down the fire of God's wrath, which shall burn up the briers and the thorns; that is, the wicked themselves. Briers and thorns are an image frequently applied in Scripture, when set on fire, to the rage of the wicked; violent, yet impotent, and of no long continuance. "They are extinct as the fire of thorns," <reference osisRef="Psa.118.12">Psa 118:12</reference>. To the wicked themselves, as useless and unprofitable, proper objects of God's wrath, to be burned up, or driven away by the wind. "As thorns cut up they shall be consumed in the fire," <reference osisRef="Isa.33.12">Isa 33:12</reference>. Both these ideas seem to be joined in <reference osisRef="Psa.58.9">Psa 58:9</reference> : - "Before your pots shall feel the thorn, <div eID="gen26951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26952" type="x-p"/> As well the green as the dry, the tempest shall bear them away." <div eID="gen26952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26953" type="x-p"/> The green and the dry is a proverbial expression, meaning all sorts of them, good and bad, great and small, etc. So Ezekiel: "Behold, I will kindle a fire, and it shall devour every green tree, and every dry tree," <reference osisRef="Eze.20.47">Eze 20:47</reference>. D'Herbelot quotes a Persian poet describing a pestilence under the image of a conflagration: "This was a lightning that, falling upon a forest, consumed there the green wood with the dry." See Harmer's Observations, Vol. II., p. 187.
entries.c4e085902bd3b633df8dc4efa43d32c0058b0b03: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen26953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26954" type="x-p"/> The flesh of his own arm "The flesh of his neighbor" - "Του βραχιονος του αδελφου αυτου, the Septuagint Alexand. Duplex versio, quarum altera legit רעו reo, quae vox extat, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.21">Jer 6:21</reference>. Nam רע rea, αδελφος, <reference osisRef="Gen.43.33">Gen 43:33</reference>. Recte ni fallor." - Secker. I add to this excellent remark, that the Chaldee manifestly reads רעו reo, his neighbor, not זרעו zeroo, his arm; for he renders it by קריביה karibeyh, his neighbor. And Jeremiah has the very same expression: ואיש בשר רעהו יאכלו veish besar reehu yochelu, "and every one shall eat the flesh of his neighbor," <reference osisRef="Jer.19.9">Jer 19:9</reference>. This observation, I think, gives the true reading and sense of this place: and the context strongly confirms it by explaining the general idea by particular instances, in the following verse: "Every man shall devour the flesh of his neighbor;" that is, they shall harass and destroy one another. "Manasseh shall destroy Ephraim, and Ephraim, Manasseh;" which two tribes were most closely connected both in blood and situation as brothers and neighbors; "and both of them in the midst of their own dissensions shall agree in preying upon Judah." The common reading, "shall devour the flesh of his own arm," in connection with what follows, seems to make either an inconsistency, or an anticlimax; whereas by this correction the following verse becomes an elegant illustration of the foregoing. - L.  <chapter eID="Isa.9"/> <div eID="gen26954" type="x-p"/>

entries.8238322099a12217198b4713c28566761417723b: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Isa 9:1</reference> <div eID="gen12924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12925" type="x-p"/> After the prophet has thus depicted the people as without morning dawn, he gives the reason for the assumption that a restoration of light is to be expected, although not for the existing generation. <hi type="italic">“For it does not remain dark where there is now distress: in the first time He brought into disgrace the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and in the last He brings to honour the road by the sea, the other side of Jordan, the circle of the Gentiles.”</hi> כּי is neither to be taken as equivalent to the untranslatable ὃτι <hi type="italic">recitativum</hi> (Knobel), nor is there any necessity to translate it “but” or “nevertheless,” and supply the clause, “it will not remain so.” The reason assigned for the fact that the unbelieving people of Judah had fallen into a night without morning, is, that there was a morning coming, whose light, however, would not rise upon the land of Judah first, but upon other parts of the land. <hi type="italic">Mū‛âp</hi> and <hi type="italic">mūzâk</hi> are <hi type="italic">hophal</hi> nouns: a state of darkness and distress. The meaning is, There is not, i.e., there will not remain, a state of darkness over the land (<hi type="italic">lâh</hi>, like <hi type="italic">bâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.21">Isa 8:21</reference>, refers to <hi type="italic">'eretz</hi>), which is now in a state of distress; but those very districts which God has hitherto caused to suffer deep humiliation He will bring to honour by and by (<hi type="italic">hēkal</hi> = <hi type="italic">hēkēl</hi>, according to Ges. §67, Anm. 3, opp. <hi type="italic">hicbı̄d</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.23.9">Isa 23:9</reference>). The height of the glorification would correspond to the depth of the disgrace. We cannot adopt Knobel’s rendering, “as at a former time,” etc., taking עת as an accusative of time and כּ as equivalent to כּאשׁר, for כּ is never used conjunctionally in this way (see Psalter, i. 301, and ii. 514); and in the examples adduced by Knobel (viz., <reference osisRef="Isa.61.11">Isa 61:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.7.2">Job 7:2</reference>), the verbal clauses after <hi type="italic">Caph</hi> are elliptical relative clauses. The rendering adopted by Rosenmüller and others (<hi type="italic">sicut tempus prius vilem reddidit</hi>, etc., “as a former time brought it into contempt”) is equally wrong. And Ewald, again, is not correct in taking the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> in <hi type="italic">v'hâ</hi>-<hi type="italic">acharōn</hi> as the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> of sequence used in the place of the <hi type="italic">Cēn</hi> of comparison. הראשׁון כּעת and האחרון are both definitions of time. The prophet intentionally indicates the time of disgrace with כּ, because this would extend over a lengthened period, in which the same fate would occur again and again. The time of glorification, on the other hand, is indicated by the <hi type="italic">accus. temporis</hi>, because it would occur but once, and then continue in perpetuity and without change. It is certainly possible that the prophet may have regarded <hi type="italic">hâ</hi>-<hi type="italic">acharōn</hi> as the subject; but this would destroy the harmony of the antithesis. By the land or territory of Naphtali (<hi type="italic">'artzâh</hi>, poet. for <hi type="italic">'eretz</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.12">Job 37:12</reference>, with a toneless <hi type="italic">ah</hi>) we are to understand the upper Galilee of later times, and by the land of Zebulun lower Galilee. In the antithetical parallel clause, what is meant by the two lands is distinctly specified: (1.) “the road by the sea,” <hi type="italic">derek hayyâm</hi>, the tract of land on the western shore of the sea of Chinnereth; (2.) “the other side of Jordan,” <hi type="italic">‛ēber hayyardēn</hi>, the country to the east of the Jordan; (3.) “the circle of the Gentiles,” <hi type="italic">gelı̄l haggōyim</hi>, the northernmost border-land of Palestine, only a portion of the so-called <hi type="italic">Galilaea</hi> of after times. Ever since the times of the judges, all these lands had been exposed, on account of the countries that joined them, to corruption from Gentile influence and subjugation by heathen foes. The northern tribes on this side, as well as those on the other side, suffered the most in the almost incessant war between Israel and the Syrians, and afterwards between Israel and the Assyrians; and the transportation of their inhabitants, which continued under Pul, Tiglath-pileser, and Shalmanassar, amounted at last to utter depopulation (Caspari, <hi type="italic">Beitr</hi>. 116-118). But these countries would be the very first that would be remembered when that morning dawn of glory should break. Matthew informs us (Mat 4:13.) in what way this was fulfilled at the commencement of the Christian times. On the ground of this prophecy of Isaiah, and not of a “somewhat mistaken exposition of it,” as Renan maintains in his <hi type="italic">Vie de Jésus</hi> (Chapter 13), the Messianic hopes of the Jewish nation were really directed towards Galilee.<note placement="foot">The Zohar was not the first to teach that the Messiah would appear in Galilee, and that redemption would break forth from Tiberias; but this is found in the Talmud and Midrash (see <hi type="italic">Litteratur-blatt des Orients</hi>, 1843, Col. 776).</note> <div eID="gen12925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12926" type="x-p"/> It is true that, according to Jerome, <hi type="italic">in loc.</hi>, the Nazarenes supposed <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Isa 9:1</reference></hi> to refer to the light of the gospel spread by the preaching of Paul <hi type="italic">in terminos gentium et viam universi maris</hi>. But “the sea” (<hi type="italic">hayyâm</hi>) cannot possibly be understood as referring to the Mediterranean, as Meier and Hofmann suppose, for “the way of the sea” (<hi type="italic">derek hayyâm</hi>) would in that case have been inhabited by the Philistines and Phoenicians; whereas the prophet’s intention was evidently to mention such Israelitish provinces as had suffered the greatest affliction and degradation.
entries.180cbaabdfc9f73f65c1c5a4d1a9e042921a0df8: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference> <div eID="gen12926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12927" type="x-p"/> The range of vision is first widened in Isa 9:2.: <hi type="italic">“The people that walk about in darkness see a great light; they who dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them a light shines.”</hi> The range of vision is here extended; not to the Gentiles, however, but to all Israel. Salvation would not break forth till it had become utterly dark along the horizon of Israel, according to the description in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.30">Isa 5:30</reference>, i.e., till the land of Jehovah had become a land of the shadow of death on account of the apostasy of its inhabitants from Jehovah (<hi type="italic">zalmâveth</hi> is modified, after the manner of a composite noun, from <hi type="italic">zalmūth</hi>, according to the form <hi type="italic">kadrūth</hi>, and is derived from צלם, Aeth. <hi type="italic">salema</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">zalima</hi>, to be dark).<note placement="foot">The shadow or shade, <hi type="italic">zēl</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">zill</hi> (radically related to <hi type="italic">tall</hi> = טל, dew), derived its name <hi type="italic">ab obtegendo</hi>, and according to the idea attached to it as the opposite of heat or of light, was used as a figure of a beneficent shelter (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.3">Isa 16:3</reference>), or of what was dark and horrible (cf., Targ. <hi type="italic">tallâni</hi>, a night-demon). The verb <hi type="italic">zâlam</hi>, in the sense of the Arabic <hi type="italic">zalima</hi>, bears the same relation to <hi type="italic">zâlal</hi> as <hi type="italic">bâham</hi> to <hi type="italic">bâhâh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gen</hi>. p. 93), <hi type="italic">‛âram</hi>, to be naked, to <hi type="italic">‛ârâh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Jeshurun</hi>, p. 159). The noun <hi type="italic">zelem</hi>, however, is either formed from this <hi type="italic">zâlam</hi>, or else directly from <hi type="italic">zēl</hi>, with the substantive termination <hi type="italic">em</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen12927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12928" type="x-p"/> The apostate mass of the nation is to be regarded as already swept away; for if death has cast its shadow over the land, it must be utterly desolate. In this state of things the remnant left in the land beholds a great light, which breaks through the sky that has been hitherto covered with blackness. The people, who turned their eyes upwards to no purpose, because they did so with cursing (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.21">Isa 8:21</reference>), are now no more. It is the remnant of Israel which sees this light of spiritual and material redemption arise above its head. In what this light would consist the prophet states afterwards, when describing first the blessings and then the star of the new time.
entries.d5b311516eff4cf19198a1416b5a2efb53f1a322: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Isa 9:3</reference> <div eID="gen12928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12929" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Isa 9:3</reference> he says, in words of thanksgiving and praise: <hi type="italic">“Thou multipliest the nation, preparest it great joy; they rejoice before Thee like the joy in harvest, as men rejoice when they share the spoil.”</hi> “The nation” (<hi type="italic">haggoi</hi>) is undoubtedly Israel, reduced to a small remnant. That God would make this again into a numerous people, was a leading feature in the pictures drawn of the time of glory (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.15">Isa 26:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.8">Isa 66:8</reference>; Zec 14:10-11), which would be in this respect the counterpart of that of Solomon (1Ki 4:20). If our explanation is the correct one so far, the only way to give an intelligible meaning to the <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> לא, taking it in a negative sense, is to render it, as Hengstenberg, Hitzig, and others have done, “Thou multipliest the nation to which Thou hadst formerly not given great joy,” which must signify, <hi type="italic">per litoten</hi>, “the nation which Thou hadst plunged into deep sorrow.” But it is unnatural to take any one of the prophetic preterites, commencing with <hi type="italic">hicbı̄d</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Isa 9:1</reference>, in any other than a future sense. We must therefore give the preference to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> לו, and render it, “Thou makest of the nation a great multitude, and preparest it great joy.” The pronoun loo is written first, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.7.7-Lev.7.9">Lev 7:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.41.4">Job 41:4</reference> (<hi type="italic">keri</hi>), probably with the emphasis assumed by Drechsler: “to it, in which there was not the smallest indication of such an issue as this.” The verbs “multiplied” (<hi type="italic">higdaltâ</hi>) and “increased” (<hi type="italic">hirbithâ</hi>) are intentionally written together, to put the intensity of the joy on a level with the extensiveness of the multitude. This joy would be a holy joy, as the expression “before Thee” implies: the expression itself recals the sacrificial meals in the courts of the temple (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.7">Deu 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.26">Deu 14:26</reference>). It would be a joy over blessings received, as the figure of the harvest indicates; and joy over evil averted, as the figure of dividing the spoil presupposes: for the division of booty is the business of conquerors. This second figure is not merely a figure: the people that are so joyous are really victorious and triumphant.<note placement="foot">On the passages in which לא <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> is לו <hi type="italic">keri</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Ps.100.3">Psa 100:3</reference> and Job 13:15.</note>
entries.cda94e871c3a22926dbc58c7543da4ab1447b530: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Isa 9:4</reference> <hi type="italic">“For the yoke of its burden and the stick of its neck, the stick of its oppressor, Thou hast broken to splinters, as in the day of Midian.”</hi> The suffixes refer to the people (<hi type="italic">hâēâm</hi>). Instead of <hi type="italic">soblō</hi>, from <hi type="italic">sōbel</hi>, we have intentionally the more musical form סבּלו (with <hi type="italic">dagesh dirimens</hi> and <hi type="italic">chateph kametz</hi> under the influence of the previous <hi type="italic">u</hi> instead of the simple <hi type="italic">sheva</hi>). The rhythm of the v. of anapaestic. “<hi type="italic">Its burden</hi>” (<hi type="italic">subbolo</hi>) and “its oppressor” (<hi type="italic">nogēs bō</hi>) both recall to mind the Egyptian bondage (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.11">Exo 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.5.6">Exo 5:6</reference>). The future deliverance, which the prophet here celebrates, would be the counterpart of the Egyptian. But as the whole of the great nation of Israel was then redeemed, whereas only a small remnant would participate in the final redemption, he compares it to the day of Midian, when Gideon broke the seven years’ dominion of Midian, not with a great army, but with a handful of resolute warriors, strong in the Lord (Judg 7). The question suggests itself here, Who is the hero, Gideon’s antitype, through whom all this is to occur? The prophet does not say; but building up one clause upon another with כּי, he gives first of all the reason for the cessation of the oppressive dominion of the imperial power - namely, the destruction of all the military stores of the enemy.
entries.6116eb715e6370f20cf500adbcc944a11c899d5e: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Isa 9:5</reference> <hi type="italic">“For every boot of those who tramp with boots in the tumult of battle, and cloak rolled in blood, shall be for burning, a food of fire.”</hi> That which is the food of fire becomes at the same time a <hi type="italic">sĕrēphâh</hi>, inasmuch as the devouring fire reduces it to ashes, and destroys its previous existence. This closing statement requires for סאון the concrete sense of a combustible thing; and this precludes such meanings as business (<hi type="italic">Handel und Wandel</hi>), noise, or din (= שׁאון, Jerome, Syriac, Rashi, and others). On the other hand, the meaning “military equipment,” adopted by Knobel and others - a meaning derived from a comparison of the derivatives of the Aramaean <hi type="italic">zūn</hi>, <hi type="italic">ăzan</hi>, and the Arabic <hi type="italic">zâna</hi>, fut. <hi type="italic">yezı̄n</hi> (to dress or equip) - would be quite admissible; at the same time, the interchange of <hi type="italic">Samech</hi> and <hi type="italic">Zain</hi> in this word cannot be dialectically established. Jos. Kimchi has very properly referred to the Targum <hi type="italic">sēn</hi>, <hi type="italic">mesân</hi> (Syr. also <hi type="italic">sâūn</hi> with an essentially long<hi type="italic">a</hi>), which signifies shoe (see Bynaeus, <hi type="italic">de calceo Hebraeorum</hi>) - a word which is more Aramaean than Hebrew, and the use of which in the present connection might be explained on the ground that the prophet had in his mind the annihilation of the Assyrian forces. We should no doubt expect <hi type="italic">sâ'ūn</hi> (<hi type="italic">sandaloumenos</hi>) instead of <hi type="italic">sō'ēn</hi>; but the denom. verb <hi type="italic">sâ'ăn</hi> might be applied to a soldier’s coming up in military boots, and so signify <hi type="italic">Caligatum venire</hi>, although the primary meaning is certainly <hi type="italic">Calceare se</hi> (e.g., <reference osisRef="Eph.6.15">Eph 6:15</reference>, Syr.). Accordingly we should render it, “every boot of him who comes booted (<hi type="italic">des Einherstiefelnden</hi>) into the tumult of battle,” taking the word <hi type="italic">ra‛ash</hi>, not as Drechsler does, in the sense of the noise made by a warrior coming up proudly in his war-boots, nor with Luzzatto in the sense of the war-boot itself, for which the word is too strong, but as referring to the noise or tumult of battle (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.22">Jer 10:22</reference>), in the midst of which the man comes up equipped or shod for military service. The prophet names the boot and garment with an obvious purpose. The destruction of the hostile weapons follows as a matter of course, if even the military shoes, worn by the soldiers in the enemies’ ranks, and the military cloaks that were lying in <hi type="italic">dâmim</hi>, i.e., in blood violently shed upon the battle-field, were all given up to the fire.
entries.c5585adda1a947a037c0e41d06750e6e98d54a74: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference> <div eID="gen12929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12930" type="x-p"/> Upon the two sentences with <hi type="italic">ci</hi> the prophet now builds a third. The reason for the triumph is the deliverance effected; and the reason for the deliverance, the destruction of the foe; and the reason for all the joy, all the freedom, all the peace, is the new great King. - <hi type="italic">“For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given; and the government rests upon His shoulder: and they call His name, Wonder, Counsellor, mighty God, Eternal-Father, Prince of Peace.”</hi> The same person whom the prophet foretold in chapter 7 as the son of the virgin who would come to maturity in troublous times, he here sees as born, and as having already taken possession of the government. There he appeared as a sign, here as a gift of grace. The prophet does not expressly say that he is a son of David in this instance any more than in chapter 7 (for the remark that has been recently made, that <hi type="italic">yeled</hi> is used here for “infant-prince,” is absurd); but this followed as a matter of course, from the fact that he was to bear the government, with all its official rights (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">Isa 22:22</reference>) and godlike majesty (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.6">Psa 21:6</reference>), upon his shoulder; for the inviolable promise of eternal sovereignty, of which the new-born infant was to be the glorious fulfilment, had been bound up with the seed of David in the course of Israel’s history ever since the declaration in 2 Sam 7. In chapter 7 it is the mother who names the child; here it is the people, or indeed any one who rejoices in him: ויּקרא, “one calls, they call, he is called,” as Luther has correctly rendered it, though under the mistaken idea that the Jews had altered the original ויּקּרא into ויּקרא, for the purpose of eliminating the Messianic sense of the passage. But the active verb itself has really been twisted by Jewish commentators in this way; so that Rashi, Kimchi, Malbim, and others follow the Targum, and explain the passage as meaning, “the God, who is called and is Wonder,' Counsellor, the mighty God, the eternal Father, calls his name the Prince of Peace;” but this rendering evidently tears asunder things that are closely connected. And Luzzatto has justly observed, that you do not expect to find attributes of God here, but such as would be characteristic of the child. He therefore renders the passage, “God the mighty, the eternal Father, the Prince of Peace, resolves upon wonderful things,” and persuades himself that this long clause is meant for the proper name of the child, just as in other cases declaratory clauses are made into proper names, e.g., the names of the prophet’s two sons. But even granting that such a sesquipedalian name were possible, in what an unskilful manner would the name be formed, since the long-winded clause, which would necessarily have to be uttered in one breath, would resolve itself again into separate clauses, which are not only names themselves, but, contrary to all expectation, names of God! The motive which prompted Luzzatto to adopt this original interpretation is worthy of notice. He had formerly endeavoured, like other commentators, to explain the passage by taking the words from “Wonderful” to “Prince of Peace” as the name of the child; and in doing this he rendered יועץ פלא “one counselling wonderful things,” thus inverting the object, and regarded “mighty God” as well as “eternal Father” as hyperbolical expressions, like the words applied to the King in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference></hi>. But now he cannot help regarding it as absolutely impossible for a human child to be called <hi type="italic">el gibbor</hi>, like God Himself in Isa 10:21. So far as the relation between his novel attempt at exposition and the accentuation is concerned, it certainly does violence to this, though not to such an extent as the other specimen of exegetical leger-demain, which makes the clause from פלא to אבי־עד the subject to ויקרא. Nevertheless, in the face of the existing accentuation, we must admit that the latter is, comparatively speaking, the better of the two; for if שמו ויקרא were intended to be the introduction to the list of names which follows, שׁמו would not be pointed with <hi type="italic">geresh</hi>, but with <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi>. The accentuators seem also to have shrunk from taking <hi type="italic">el gibbor</hi> as the name of a man. They insert intermediate points, as though “eternal Father, Prince of Peace,” were the name of the child, and all that precedes, from “Wonder” onwards, the name of God, who would call him by these two honourable names. But, at the very outset, it is improbable that there should be two names instead of one or more; and it is impossible to conceive for what precise reason such a periphrastic description of God should be employed in connection with the naming of this child, as is not only altogether different from Isaiah’s usual custom, but altogether unparalleled in itself, especially without the definite article. The names of God should at least have been defined thus, הגּבּור פּלא היּועץ, so as to distinguish them from the two names of the child. <div eID="gen12930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12931" type="x-p"/> Even assuming, therefore, that the accentuation is meant to convey this sense, “And the wonderful Counsellor, the mighty God, calls his name Eternal-Father, Prince of Peace,” as appears to be the case; we must necessarily reject it, as resting upon a misunderstanding and misinterpretation.<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">telisha</hi> in פלא is the smallest of all disjunctive accents; the geresh in שׁמו separates rather more strongly than this; the <hi type="italic">pashta</hi> in יועץ separates somewhat more than the other two, but less than the <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi> in גבור; and this <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi> is the greatest divider in the sentence. The whole sentence, therefore, distributes itself in the following manner:  אבי־עד  גבור אל  יועץ  פלא  שׁמו ויקרא שׂר־שלום . All the words from ויקרא onwards are subordinate to the <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi> attached to גבור, which is, to all appearance, intended to have the force of an introductory colon: as, for example, in <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.5">2Sa 18:5</reference> (in the case of לאמר in the clause לאמר ואת־אתי ואת־אבישי יואב). In smaller subdivisions, again, פלא (<hi type="italic">telisha</hi>) is connected with יועץ (<hi type="italic">pashta</hi>), and both together with גבור אל (<hi type="italic">munach zakeph</hi>). If only <hi type="italic">sar shalom</hi> (Prince of Peace) were intended as the name of the child, it would necessarily be accentuated in the following manner: שמו ויקרא <hi type="italic">kadma</hi> <hi type="italic">geresh</hi>, יועץ פלא <hi type="italic">teilsha</hi> <hi type="italic">gershayim</hi>, גבור אל <hi type="italic">mercha</hi> <hi type="italic">tebir</hi>, עד אבי <hi type="italic">tifchah</hi>, שׂר־שׁלום <hi type="italic">silluk</hi>; and the principal disjunctive would stand at עד instead of גבור. But if the name of the child were intended to form a declaratory clause, commencing with יועץ פלא, “determines wonderful things,” as Luzzatto assumes, we should expect to find a stronger disjunctive than <hi type="italic">telisha</hi> at פלא, the watchword of the whole; and above all, we should expect a <hi type="italic">zakeph</hi> at שׁמו, and not at גבור. This also applies to our (the ordinary) explanation. It does not correspond to the accentuation. The introductory words שׁמו ויקרא ought to have a stronger distinctive accent, in order that all which follows might stand as the name which they introduce. Francke (see <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, ii. 521) perceived this, and in his <hi type="italic">Abyssus mysteriorum Esa</hi> (ix. 6) he lays great stress upon the fact, that God who gives the name has Himself a threefold name.</note> <div eID="gen12931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12932" type="x-p"/> We regard the whole, from פלא onwards - as the connection, the expression, and the syntax require - as a dependent accusative predicate to שמו ויקרא (they call his name), which stands at the head (compare קרא, they call, it is called, in <reference osisRef="Gen.11.9">Gen 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.16.14">Gen 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.7.26">Jos 7:26</reference>, and above <reference osisRef="Isa.8.4">Isa 8:4</reference>, ישׂא, they will carry: Ges. §137, 3). If it be urged, as an objection to the Messianic interpretation of <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14-Isa.7.15">Isa 7:14-15</reference>, that the Christ who appeared was not named Immanuel, but Jesus, this objection is sufficiently met by the fact that He did not receive as a proper name any one of the five names by which, according to this second prophecy, He was to be called. Moreover, this objection would apply quite as strongly to the notion, which has been a very favourite one with Jewish commentators (e.g., Rashi, A. E. Kimchi, Abravanel, Malbim, Luzzatto, and others), and even with certain Christian commentators (such as Grotius, Gesenius, etc.), that the prophecy refers to Hezekiah - a notion which is a disgrace to those who thereby lead both themselves and others astray. For even if the hopes held out in the prophecy were attached for a long time to Hezekiah, the mistake was but too quickly discovered; whereas the commentators in question perpetuate the mistake, by forcing it upon the prophecy itself, although the prophet, even after the deception had been outlived, not only did not suppress the prophecy, but handed it down to succeeding ages as awaiting a future and infallible fulfilment. For the words in their strict meaning point to the Messiah, whom men may for a time, with pardonable error, have hoped to find in Hezekiah, but whom, with unpardonable error, men refused to acknowledge, even when He actually appeared in Jesus. The name Jesus is the combination of all the Old Testament titles used to designate the Coming One according to His nature and His works. The names contained in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Isa 7:14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference> are not thereby suppressed; but they have continued, from the time of Mary downwards, in the mouths of all believers. There is not one of these names under which worship and homage have not been paid to Him. But we never find them crowded together anywhere else, as we do here in Isaiah; and in this respect also our prophet proves himself the greatest of the Old Testament evangelists. <div eID="gen12932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12933" type="x-p"/> The first name is פּלא, or perhaps more correctly פּלא, which is not to be taken in connection with the next word, יועץ, though this construction might seem to commend itself in accordance with עצה הפליא, in Isa 28:29. This is the way in which it has been taken by the Seventy and others (thus lxx, θαυμαστὸς σύμβουλος; Theodoret, θαυμαστῶς βουλεύων). If we adopted this explanation, we might regard יועץ פלא as an inverted form for פלא יועץ: counselling wonderful things. The possibility of such an inversion is apparent from <reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Isa 22:2</reference>, מלאה תשׁאות, i.e., full of tumult. Or, following the analogy of <hi type="italic">pere' âdâm</hi> (a wild man) in <reference osisRef="Gen.16.12">Gen 16:12</reference>, we might regard it as a genitive construction: a wonder of a counsellor; in which case the disjunctive <hi type="italic">teilshâh</hi> <hi type="italic">gedolâh</hi> in <hi type="italic">pele'</hi> would have to be exchanged for a connecting <hi type="italic">mahpach</hi>. Both combinations have their doubtful points, and, so far as the sense is concerned, would lead us rather to expect עצה מפליא; whereas there is nothing at all to prevent our taking פלא and יועץ as two separate names (not even the accentuation, which is without parallel elsewhere, so far as the combination of <hi type="italic">pashta</hi> with <hi type="italic">teilshah</hi> is concerned, and therefore altogether unique). Just as the angel of Jehovah, when asked by Manoah what was his name (Jdg 13:18), replied פּלי (פּלאי), and indicated thereby his divine nature - a nature incomprehensible to mortal men; so here the God-given ruler is also <hi type="italic">pele'</hi>, a phenomenon lying altogether beyond human conception or natural occurrence. Not only is this or that wonderful in Him; but He Himself is throughout a wonder - παραδοξασμός, as Symmachus renders it. The second name if <hi type="italic">yō‛ētz</hi>, counsellor, because, by virtue of the spirit of counsel which He possesses (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference>), He can always discern and given counsel for the good of His nation. There is no need for Him to surround Himself with counsellors; but without receiving counsel at all, He counsels those that are without counsel, and is thus the end of all want of counsel to His nation as a whole. The third name, <hi type="italic">El</hi> <hi type="italic">gibbor</hi>, attributes divinity to Him. Not, indeed, if we render the words “Strength, Hero,” as Luther does; or “Hero of Strength,” as Meier has done; or “a God of a hero,” as Hofmann proposes; or “Hero-God,” i.e., one who fights and conquers like an invincible god, as Ewald does. But all these renderings, and others of a similar kind, founder, without needing any further refutation, on <reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">Isa 10:21</reference>, where He, to whom the remnant of Israel will turn with penitence, is called <hi type="italic">El</hi> <hi type="italic">gibbor</hi> (the mighty God). There is no reason why we should take <hi type="italic">El</hi> in this name of the Messiah in any other sense than in <hi type="italic">Immanu</hi>-<hi type="italic">El</hi>; not to mention the fact that <hi type="italic">El</hi> in Isaiah is always a name of God, and that the prophet was ever strongly conscious of the antithesis between <hi type="italic">El</hi> and <hi type="italic">âdâm</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">Isa 31:3</reference> (cf., Hos 11:9) clearly shows. And finally, <hi type="italic">El gibbor</hi> was a traditional name of God, which occurs as early as <reference osisRef="Deut.10.17">Deu 10:17</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.32.18">Jer 32:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.32">Neh 9:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.8">Psa 24:8</reference>, etc. The name <hi type="italic">gibbor</hi> is used here as an adjective, like <hi type="italic">shaddai</hi> in <hi type="italic">El shaddai</hi>. The Messiah, then, is here designated “mighty God.” Undoubtedly this appears to go beyond the limits of the Old Testament horizon; but what if it should go beyond them? It stands written once for all, just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference> <hi type="italic">Jehovah Zidkenu</hi> (Jehovah our Righteousness) is also used as a name of the Messiah - a Messianic name, which even the synagogue cannot set aside (vid., <hi type="italic">Midrash Mishle </hi>57 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, where this is adduced as one of the eight names of the Messiah). Still we must not go too far. If we look at the spirit of the prophecy, the mystery of the incarnation of God is unquestionably indicated in such statements as these. But if we look at the consciousness of the prophet himself, nothing further was involved than this, that the Messiah would be the image of God as no other man ever had been (cf., <hi type="italic">El</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">Psa 82:1</reference>), and that He would have God dwelling within Him (cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.33.16">Jer 33:16</reference>). Who else would lead Israel to victory over the hostile world, than God the mighty? The Messiah is the corporeal presence of this mighty God; for He is with Him, He is in Him, and in Him He is with Israel. The expression did not preclude the fact that the Messiah would be God and man in one person; but it did not penetrate to this depth, so far as the Old Testament consciousness was concerned. The fourth name springs out of the third: אבי־עד, eternal Father (not Booty Father, with which Hitzig and Knobel content themselves); for what is divine must be eternal. The title Eternal Father designates Him, however, not only as the possessor of eternity (Hengstenberg), but as the tender, faithful, and wise trainer, guardian, and provider for His people even in eternity (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.21">Isa 22:21</reference>). He is eternal Father, as the eternal, loving King, according to the description in Ps 72. Now, if He is mighty God, and uses His divine might in eternity for the good of His people, He is also, as the fifth name affirms, sar-<hi type="italic">shâl</hi>, a Prince who removes all peace-disturbing powers, and secures peace among the nations (Zec 9:10) - who is, as it were, the embodiment of peace come down into the world of nations (Mic 5:4). To exalt the government of David into an eternal rule of peace, is the end for which He is born; and moreover He proves Himself to be what He is not only called, but actually is.
entries.3745809917d084bc380e91ace18a734b6832cbfc: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Isa 9:7</reference> <hi type="italic">“To the increase of government and to peace without end, upon the throne of David, and over his Kingdom, to strengthen it, and to support it through judgment and righteousness from henceforth even for ever. The jealousy of Jehovah of hosts will fulfil this.”</hi> למרבּה (written with <hi type="italic">Mêm clausum</hi> in the middle of the one word, and, according to Elias Levita, properly to be read רבּה לם, <hi type="italic">iis magnificando</hi>, in accordance with this way of writing the word)<note placement="foot">When Bar-Kappara says (b. <hi type="italic">Sanhedrin</hi> 94 <hi type="italic">a</hi>) that God designed to make Hezekiah the Messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog, but that Hezekiah was not found worthy of this, and therefore the <hi type="italic">Mem</hi> of <hi type="italic">l'marbeh</hi> was closed, there is so far some sense in this, that the Messianic hopes really could centre for a certain time in Hezekiah; whereas the assertion of a certain Hillel (<hi type="italic">ib</hi>. 98 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), that Hezekiah was actually the Messiah of Israel, and no other was to be expected, is nothing but the perverted fancy of an empty brain. For an instance of the opposite, see <reference osisRef="Neh.2.13">Neh 2:13</reference>, פרוצים הם, on which passage the Midrash observes, “The broken walls of Jerusalem will be closed in the day of salvation, and the government which has been closed up to the time of the King Messiah will be opened then.”)</note> is not a participle here, but a substantive after the forms מראה, מעשׂה, and that not from הרבּה, but from רבה, an infinitive noun expressing, according to its formation, the practical result of an action, rather than the abstract idea.<note placement="foot">We have already observed at p. 101, that this substantive formation had not a purely abstract meaning even at the first. Fürst has given the correct explanation in his <hi type="italic">Lehrgebäude der Aram. Idiome</hi>, §130.</note> <div eID="gen12933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12934" type="x-p"/> Ever extending dominion and endless peace will be brought in by the sublime and lofty King’s Son, when He sits upon the throne of David and rules over David’s kingdom. He is a <hi type="italic">semper Augustus</hi>, i.e., a perpetual increaser of the kingdom; not by war, however, but with the spiritual weapons of peace. And within He gives to the kingdom “judgment” (<hi type="italic">mishpât</hi>) and “righteousness” (<hi type="italic">zedâkâh</hi>), as the foundations and pillars of its durability: <hi type="italic">mishpât</hi>, judgment or right, which He pronounces and ordains; and righteousness, which He not only exercises Himself, but transfers to the members of His kingdom. This new epoch of Davidic sovereignty was still only a matter of faith and hope. But the zeal of Jehovah was the guarantee of its realization. The accentuation is likely to mislead here, inasmuch as it makes it appear as though the words “from henceforth even for ever” (<hi type="italic">me‛attâh v‛ad ōlâm</hi>) belonged to the closing sentence, whereas the eternal perspective which they open applies directly to the reign of the great Son of David, and only indirectly to the work of the divine jealousy. “<hi type="italic">Zeal</hi>,” or <hi type="italic">jealousy</hi>, <hi type="italic">kin'âh</hi>, lit., glowing fire, from קנּא, Arab. <hi type="italic">kanaa</hi>, to be deep red (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.24">Deu 4:24</reference>), is one of the deepest of the Old Testament ideas, and one of the most fruitful in relation to the work of reconciliation. It is two-sided. The fire of love has for its obverse the fire of wrath. For jealousy contends for the object of its love against everything that touches either the object or the love itself.<note placement="foot">Cf., Weber, <hi type="italic">On the Wrath of God</hi> (p. xxxv). It is evident that by <hi type="italic">kin'âh</hi>, ζῆλος, we are to understand the energy of love following up its violated claims upon the creature, from the comparison so common in the Scriptures between the love of God to His church and connubial affection. It is the jealousy of absolute love, which seeks to be loved in return, and indeed demands undivided love, and asserts its claim to reciprocity of love wherever this claim is refused. In a word, it is the self-vindication of scornful love. But this idea includes not only jealousy seeking the recovery of what it has lost, but also jealousy that consumes what cannot be saved (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.2">Nah 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.27">Heb 10:27</reference>); and the Scriptures therefore deduce the wrath, by which the love resisted affirms itself, and the wrath which meets those who have resisted love in the form of absolute hostility-in other words, the jealousy of love as well as the jealousy of hatred-not from love and holiness as two entirely distinct sources, but from the single source of absolute holy love, which, just because it is absolute and holy, repels and excludes whatever will not suffer itself to be embraced (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.19">Jos 24:19</reference>).</note> <div eID="gen12934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12935" type="x-p"/> Jehovah loves His nation. That He should leave it in the hands of such bad Davidic kings as Ahaz, and give it up to the imperial power of the world, would be altogether irreconcilable with this love, if continued long. But His love flares up, consumes all that is adverse, and gives to His people the true King, in whom that which was only foreshadowed in David and Solomon reaches its highest antitypical fulfilment. With the very same words, “the zeal of Jehovah of hosts,” etc., Isaiah seals the promise in Isa 37:32.
entries.714a62ab26cfd200d1dfd98fb5742bb9255c74f8: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8-Isa.9.12">Isa 9:8-12</reference> <div eID="gen12935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12936" type="x-p"/> The great light would not arise till the darkness had reached its deepest point. The gradual increase of this darkness is predicted in this second section of the esoteric addresses. Many difficult questions suggest themselves in connection with this section. 1. Is it directed against the northern kingdom only, or against all Israel? 2. What was the historical standpoint of the prophet himself? The majority of commentators reply that the prophet is only prophesying against Ephraim here, and that Syria and Ephraim have already been chastised by Tiglath-pileser. The former is incorrect. The prophet does indeed commence with Ephraim, but he does not stop there. The fates of both kingdoms flow into one another here, as well as in Isa 8:5., just as they were causally connected in actual fact. And it cannot be maintained, that when the prophet uttered his predictions Ephraim had already felt the scourging of Tiglath-pileser. The prophet takes his stand at a time when judgment after judgment had fallen upon all Israel without improving it. And one of these past judgments was the scourging of Ephraim by Tiglath-pileser. How much or how little of the events which the prophet looks back upon from this ideal standpoint had already taken place, it is impossible to determine; but this is a matter of indifference so far as the prophecy is concerned. The prophet, from his ideal standing-place, had not only this or that behind him, but all that is expressed in this section by perfects and aorists (Ges. §129, 2,<hi type="italic">b</hi>). And we already know from <reference osisRef="Isa.2.9">Isa 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference>, that he sued the future conversive as the preterite of the ideal past. We therefore translate the whole in the present tense. In outward arrangement there is no section of Isaiah so symmetrical as this. In chapter 5 we found one partial approach to the strophe in similarity of commencement, and another in chapter 2 in similarity of conclusion. But here <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference></hi> is adapted as the <hi type="italic">refrain</hi> of four symmetrical strophes. We will take each strophe by itself. <div eID="gen12936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12937" type="x-p"/> Strophe 1. <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8-Isa.9.12">Isa 9:8-12</reference> “<hi type="italic">The Lord sends out a word against Jacob, and it descends into Israel. And all the people must make atonement, Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, saying in pride and haughtiness of heart, 'Bricks are fallen down, and we build with square stones; sycamores are hewn down, and we put cedars in their place.' Jehovah raises Rezin’s oppressors high above him, and pricks up his enemies: Aram from the east, and Philistines from the west; they devour Israel with full mouth. For all this His anger is not turned away, and His hand is stretched out still</hi>.” The <hi type="italic">word</hi> (<hi type="italic">dâbâr</hi>) is both in nature and history the messenger of the Lord: it runs quickly through the earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.15">Psa 147:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.18">Psa 147:18</reference>), and when sent by the Lord, comes to men to destroy or to heal (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.20">Psa 107:20</reference>), and never returns to its sender void (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.10-Isa.55.11">Isa 55:10-11</reference>). Thus does the Lord now send a word against Jacob (<hi type="italic">Jacob</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.5">Isa 2:5</reference>); and this heavenly messenger descends into Israel (<hi type="italic">nâphal</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.4.28">Dan 4:28</reference>, and like the Arabic <hi type="italic">nazala</hi>, which is the word usually employed to denote the communication of divine revelation), taking shelter, as it were, in the soul of the prophet. Its immediate commission is directed against Ephraim, which has been so little humbled by the calamities that have fallen upon it since the time of Jehu, that the people are boasting that they will replace bricks and sycamores (or sycamines, from <hi type="italic">shikmin</hi>), that wide-spread tree (1Ki 10:27), with works of art and cedars. “<hi type="italic">We put in their place:</hi>” <hi type="italic">nachaliph</hi> is not used here as in <reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job 14:7</reference>, where it signifies to sprout again (<hi type="italic">nova germina emittere</hi>), but as in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.1">Isa 41:1</reference>, where it is construed with כּח (strength), and signifies to renew (<hi type="italic">novas vires assumere</hi>). In this instance, when the object is one external to the subject, the meaning is to substitute (<hi type="italic">substituere</hi>), like the Arabic <hi type="italic">achlafa</hi>, to restore. The poorest style of building in the land is contrasted with the best; for “the sycamore is a tree which only flourishes in the plain, and there the most wretched houses are still built of bricks dried in the sun, and of knotty beams of sycamore.”<note placement="foot">Rosen, <hi type="italic">Topographisches aus Jerusalem</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen12937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12938" type="x-p"/> These might have been destroyed by the war, but more durable and stately buildings would rise up in their place. Ephraim, however, would be made to feel this defiance of the judgments of God (to “know,” as in Hos 9:7; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.14">Eze 25:14</reference>). Jehovah would give the adversaries of Rezin authority over Ephraim, and instigate his foes: <hi type="italic">sicsēc</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">Isa 19:2</reference>, from <hi type="italic">sâcac</hi>, in its primary sense of “prick,” <hi type="italic">figere</hi>, which has nothing to do with the meanings to plait and cover, but from which we have the words שׂך, סך, a thorn, nail, or plug, and which is probably related to שׂכה, to view, lit., to fix; hence <hi type="italic">pilpel</hi>, to prick up, incite, which is the rendering adopted by the Targum here and in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">Isa 19:2</reference>, and by the lxx at Isa 19:2. There is no necessity to quote the talmudic <hi type="italic">sicsēc</hi>, to kindle (by friction), which is never met with in the metaphorical sense of exciting. It would be even better to take our <hi type="italic">sicsēc</hi> as an intensive form of <hi type="italic">sâcac</hi>, used in the same sense as the Arabic, viz., to provide one’s self with weapons, to arm; but this is probably a denominative from <hi type="italic">sicca</hi>, signifying offensive armour, with the idea of pricking and spearing - a radical notion, from which it would be easy to get at the satisfactory meaning, to spur on or instigate. “The oppressors of <hi type="italic">Rezin</hi>” <hi type="italic">tzâr</hi> <hi type="italic">Retzı̄n</hi>, a simple play upon the words, like <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> <hi type="italic">goi</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>, and many others in Isaiah) are the Assyrians, whose help had been sought by Ahaz against Rezin; though perhaps not these exclusively, but possibly also the Trachonites, for example, against whom the mountain fortress <hi type="italic">Rezı̄n</hi> appears to have been erected, to protect the rich lands of eastern Hauran. In <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">Isa 9:12</reference> the range of vision stretches over all Israel. It cannot be otherwise, for the northern kingdom never suffered anything from the Philistines; whereas an invasion of Judah by the Philistines was really one of the judgments belonging to the time of Ahaz (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.16-2Chr.28.19">2Ch 28:16-19</reference>). Consequently by <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> here we are to understand all Israel, the two halves of which would become a rich prize to the enemy. Ephraim would be swallowed up by Aram - namely, by those who had been subjugated by Asshur, and were now tributary to it - and Judah would be swallowed up by the Philistines. But this strait would be very far from being the end of the punishments of God. Because Israel would not turn, the wrath of God would not turn away.
entries.a055f22be490aeb69b14be2b321ed9f16fbac014: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13-Isa.9.17">Isa 9:13-17</reference> <div eID="gen12938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12939" type="x-p"/> Strophe 2. <hi type="italic">“But the people turneth not unto Him that smiteth it, and they seek not Jehovah of hosts. Therefore Jehovah rooteth out of Israel head and tail, palm-branch and rush, in one day. Elders and highly distinguished men, this is the head; and prophets, lying teachers, this is the tail. The leaders of this people have become leaders astray, and their followers swallowed up. Therefore the Lord will not rejoice in their young men, and will have no compassion on their orphans and widows: for all together are profligate and evil-doers, and every mouth speaketh blasphemy. With all this His anger is not turned away, and His hand is stretched out still.”</hi> As the first stage of the judgments has been followed by no true conversion to Jehovah the almighty judge, there comes a second. עד שׁוּב (to turn unto) denotes a thorough conversion, not stopping half-way. “The smiter of it” (<hi type="italic">hammaccēhu</hi>), or “he who smiteth it,” it Jehovah (compare, on the other hand, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.20">Isa 10:20</reference>, where Asshur is intended). The article and suffix are used together, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.24.2">Isa 24:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">Pro 16:4</reference> (vid., Ges. §110, 2; Caspari, <hi type="italic">Arab. Gram</hi>. §472). But there was coming now a great day of punishment (in the view of the prophet, it was already past), such as Israel experienced more than once in the Assyrian oppressions, and Judah in the Chaldean, when head and tail, or, according to another proverbial expression, palm-branch and rush, would be rooted out. We might suppose that the persons referred to were the high and low; but <reference osisRef="Isa.9.15">Isa 9:15</reference> makes a different application of the first double figure, by giving it a different turn from its popular sense (compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">er</hi>-<hi type="italic">ru 'ūs w</hi>-<hi type="italic">aledhnâb</hi> = lofty and low, in Dietrich, <hi type="italic">Abhandlung</hi>, p. 209). The opinion which has very widely prevailed since the time of Koppe, that this v. is a gloss, is no doubt a very natural one (see Hitzig, <hi type="italic">Begriff der Kritik</hi>; Ewald, <hi type="italic">Propheten</hi>, i. 57). But Isaiah’s custom of supplying his own gloss is opposed to such a view; also Isaiah’s composition in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.3">Isa 3:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.30.20">Isa 30:20</reference>, and the relation in which this v. stands to <reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Isa 9:16</reference>; and lastly, the singular character of the gloss itself, which is one of the strongest proofs that it contains the prophet’s exposition of his own words. The chiefs of the nation were the head of the national body; and behind, like a wagging dog’s tail, sat the false prophets with their flatteries of the people, loving, as Persius says, <hi type="italic">blando caudam jactare popello</hi>. The prophet drops the figure of <hi type="italic">Cippâh</hi>, the palm-branch which forms the crown of the palm, and which derives its name from the fact that it resembles the palm of the hand (<hi type="italic">instar palmae manus</hi>), and <hi type="italic">agmōn</hi>, the rush which grows in the marsh.<note placement="foot">The noun <hi type="italic">agam</hi> is used in the Old Testament as well as in the Talmud to signify both a marshy place (see <hi type="italic">Baba mesi'a</hi> 36b, and more especially <hi type="italic">Aboda zara</hi> 38 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, where <hi type="italic">giloi agmah</hi> signifies the laying bare of the marshy soil by the burning up of the reeds), and also the marsh grass (<hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi> 11 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, “if all the <hi type="italic">agmim</hi> were <hi type="italic">kalams</hi>, i.e., writing reeds, or pens;” and <hi type="italic">Kiddûsin</hi> 62b, where agam signifies a talk of marsh-grass or reed, a rush or bulrush, and is explained, with a reference to <reference osisRef="Isa.58.5">Isa 58:5</reference>, as signifying a tender, weak stalk). The noun <hi type="italic">agmon</hi>, on the other hand, signifies only the stalk of the marsh-grass, or the marsh-grass itself; and in this sense it is not found in the Talmud (see <hi type="italic">Comm on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Isa.41.10-Isa.41.13">Isa 41:10-13</reference>). The verbal meaning upon which these names are founded is evident from the Arabic <hi type="italic">mâ āgim</hi> (<hi type="italic">magūm</hi>), “bad water” (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.19.10">Isa 19:10</reference>). There is no connection between this and <hi type="italic">maugil</hi>, literally a depression of the soil, in which water lodges for a long time, and which is only dried up in summer weather.</note> <div eID="gen12939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12940" type="x-p"/> The allusion here is to the rulers of the nation and the dregs of the people. The basest extremity were the demagogues in the shape of prophets. For it had come to this, as <reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Isa 9:16</reference> affirms, that those who promised to lead by a straight road led astray, and those who suffered themselves to be led by them were as good as already swallowed up by hell (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.12">Isa 3:12</reference>). Therefore the Sovereign Ruler would not rejoice over the young men of this nation; that is to say, He would suffer them to be smitten by their enemies, without going with them to battle, and would refuse His customary compassion even towards widows and orphans, for they were all thoroughly corrupt on every side. The alienation, obliquity, and dishonesty of their heart, are indicated by the word <hi type="italic">Chânēph</hi> (from <hi type="italic">Chânaph</hi>, which has in itself the indifferent radical idea of inclination; so that in Arabic, <hi type="italic">Chanı̄f</hi>, as a synonym of <hi type="italic">‛âdil</hi>,<note placement="foot">This is the way in which it should be written in <hi type="italic">Comm on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Isa.13.16">Isa 13:16</reference>; <hi type="italic">‛adala</hi> has also the indifferent meaning of return or decision.</note> has the very opposite meaning of decision in favour of what is right); the badness of their actions by מרע (in half pause for מרע<note placement="foot">Nevertheless this reading is also met with, and according to <hi type="italic">Masora finalis</hi>, p. 52, col. 8, this is the correct reading (as in <reference osisRef="Prov.17.4">Pro 17:4</reference>, where it is doubtful whether the meaning is a friend or a malevolent person). The question is not an unimportant one, as we may see from Olshausen, §258, p. 581.</note> = מרע, <hi type="italic">maleficus</hi>); the vicious infatuation of their words by <hi type="italic">nebâlâh</hi>. This they are, and this they continue; and consequently the wrathful hand of God is stretched out over them for the infliction of fresh strokes.
entries.e6b5725b73b81091254f0d93a781d8c56fd1e4ee: <reference osisRef="Isa.9.18-Isa.9.21">Isa 9:18-21</reference> <div eID="gen12940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12941" type="x-p"/> Strophe 3. <hi type="italic">“For the wickedness burneth up like fire: it devours thorns and thistles, and burns in the thickets of the wood; and they smoke upwards in a lofty volume of smoke. Through the wrath of Jehovah of hosts the land is turned into coal, and the nation has become like the food of fire: not one spares his brother. They hew on the right, and are hungry; and devour on the left, and are not satisfied: they devour the flesh of their own arm: Manasseh, Ephraim; and Ephraim, Manasseh: these together over Judah. With all this His anger is not turned away, and His hand is stretched out still.”</hi> The standpoint of the prophet is at the extreme end of the course of judgment, and from that he looks back. Consequently this link of the chain is also past in his view, and hence the future conversives. The curse, which the apostasy of Israel carries within itself, now breaks fully out. Wickedness, i.e., the constant thirst of evil, is a fire which a man kindles in himself. And when the grace of God, which damps and restrains this fire, is all over, it is sure to burst forth: the wickedness bursts forth like fire (the verb is used here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Isa 30:27</reference>, with reference to the wrath of God). And this is the case with the wickedness of Israel, which now consumes first of all thorns and thistles, i.e., individual sinners who are the most ripe for judgment, upon whom the judgment commences, and then the thicket of the wood (<hi type="italic">sib</hi>-<hi type="italic">che</hi>,<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">metheg</hi> (<hi type="italic">gaya</hi>) in סבכי (to be pronounced <hi type="italic">sib</hi>-<hi type="italic">che</hi>) has simply the caphonic effect of securing a distinct enunciation to the sibilant letter (in other instances to the guttural, vid., <hi type="italic">‛arboth</hi>, Num 31:12), in cases where the second syllable of the word commences with a guttural or labial letter, or with an aspirate.</note> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">Isa 10:34</reference>, from <hi type="italic">sebac</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.13">Gen 22:13</reference> = <hi type="italic">sobec</hi>), that is to say, the great mass of the people, which is woven together by bands of iniquity (<hi type="italic">vattizzath</hi> is not a reflective <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, as in 2Ki 22:13, but <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, to kindle into anything, i.e., to set it on fire). The contrast intended in the two figures is consequently not the high and low (Ewald), nor the useless and useful (Drechsler), but individuals and the whole (Vitringa). The fire, into which the wickedness bursts out, seizes individuals first of all; and then, like a forest fire, it seizes upon the nation at large in all its ranks and members, who “<hi type="italic">whirl up</hi> (roll up) <hi type="italic">ascending of smoke</hi>,” i.e., who roll up in the form of ascending smoke (<hi type="italic">hith'abbek</hi>, a synonym of <hi type="italic">hithhappēk</hi>, Jdg 7:13, to curl or roll). This fire of wickedness was no other than the wrath (<hi type="italic">ebrâh</hi>) of God: it is God’s own wrath, for all sin carries this within itself as its own self-punishment. By this fire of wrath the soil of the land is gradually but thoroughly burnt out, and the people of the land utterly consumed: עתם ἁπ λεγ to be red-hot (lxx συγκέκαυται, also the Targum), and to be dark or black (Arabic <hi type="italic">‛atame</hi>, late at night), for what is burnt out becomes black. Fire and darkness are therefore correlative terms throughout the whole of the Scriptures. So far do the figures extend, in which the prophet presents the inmost essence of this stage of judgment. In its historical manifestation it consisted in the most inhuman self-destruction during an anarchical civil war. Destitute of any tender emotions, they devoured one another without being satisfied: <hi type="italic">gâzar</hi>, to cut, to hew (hence the Arabic for a butcher): <hi type="italic">zero'o</hi>, <hi type="italic">his arm</hi>, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.19.9">Jer 19:9</reference>, equivalent to the member of his own family and tribe, who was figuratively called his arm (Arabic <hi type="italic">‛adud</hi>: see Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 433), as being the natural protector and support. This interminable self-immolation, and the regicide associated with the jealousy of the different tribes, shook the northern kingdom again and again to its utter destruction. And the readiness with which the unbrotherly feelings of the northern tribes towards one another could turn into combined hostility towards Judah, was evident enough from the Syro-Ephraimitish war, the consequences of which had not passed away at the time when these prophecies were uttered. This hostility on the part of the brother kingdoms would still further increase. And the end of the judgments of wrath had not come yet.  <chapter eID="Isa.9"/> <div eID="gen12941" type="x-p"/>

entries.040ac7ea1ec56a93e67731885fcd76aa026471a1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.9.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.9.1" sID="gen41726" type="section"/> <div sID="gen41727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Yet the darkness shall not be.</hi> He begins to comfort the wretched by the hope of alleviation, that they may not be swallowed up by the huge mass of distresses. Many take these words in quite an opposite meaning, that is, as a threatening which denounces against the Jews a heavier affliction than that with which Tiglath-pileser (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</reference>) and Shalmanezer (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:6</reference>) afflicted them. The former inflicted a heavy calamity, the latter inflicted one still heavier, for he carried the twelve tribes into captivity, and blotted out the name of the nation. Some think that he now foretells the heaviest calamity of all, for if it be compared with the former two, it exceeds both of them. Though I am not prepared to reject this view, for it does not want plausibility, yet I rather favor a different opinion. The other interpretation is indeed more plausible, that the Prophet intended to deprive hypocrites of every enjoyment, that they might not imagine that this calamity would quickly pass away like a storm as the others had done, for it would be utterly destructive; and so we shall take the particle <foreign xml:lang="he">כי</foreign> (<hi type="italic">ki</hi>) in its literal meaning. <note n="138"> <div sID="gen41728" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew particle <foreign xml:lang="he">כי</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">ki</hi>,) which is placed at the beginning of this verse, is rendered in the English version by <hi type="italic">Nevertheless</hi>; but Calvin says that he is willing to translate it <hi type="italic">for</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen41728" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen41727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41729" type="x-p"/>But in my opinion it is most appropriate to view it as a consolation, in which he begins to mitigate what he had said about that frightful <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> and <hi type="italic">driving</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.8.22">Isaiah 8:22</reference>,) and, by allaying the bitterness of those punishments, encourages them to expect the favor of God. As if he had said, “<hi type="italic">and yet</hi>, amidst that shocking calamity which the Jews shall endure, <hi type="italic">the darkness will not be such as when</hi> the land of Israel was afflicted, first, by Tiglath-pileser, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</reference>,) and afterwards more grievously by Shalmanezer,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:6</reference>.) Amidst so great extremities believers might otherwise have fainted, if their hearts had not been cheered by some consolation. Isaiah therefore directs his discourse to them lest they should think that they were ruined, for he intimates that the chastisements which are now to be inflicted will be lighter than those which came before. That this is the natural interpretation will quickly appear from what immediately follows.<div eID="gen41729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41730" type="x-p"/>But why does the Prophet say that this calamity, which was far more dreadful, would be more mild and gentle? For Jerusalem was to be razed, the temple thrown down, and the sacrifices abolished, which had remained untouched during the former calamities. It might be thought that these were the severest of all, and that the former, in comparison of them, were light. But it ought to be observed, that while in the former instances there was no promise, an explicit promise was added to this threatening. By this alone can temptations be overcome and chastisements be rendered light. By this seasoning alone, I say, are our afflictions alleviated; and all who are destitute of it must despair. But if, by means of it, the Lord strengthen us by holding out the hope of assistance, there is no affliction so heavy that we shall not reckon it to be light.<div eID="gen41730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41731" type="x-p"/>This may be made plain by a comparison. A man may happen to be drowned in a small stream, and yet, though he had fallen into the open sea, if he had got hold of a plank he might have been rescued and brought on shore. In like manner the slightest calamities will overwhelm us if we are deprived of God’s favor; but if we relied on the word of God, we might come out of the heaviest calamity safe and uninjured.<div eID="gen41731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41732" type="x-p"/>As to the words, some take <foreign xml:lang="he">מועף</foreign> (<hi type="italic">mugnaph</hi>) for an adjective, as if the Prophet said,<hi type="italic"> It shall not be darkened</hi>; but the feminine pronoun which immediately follows, <foreign xml:lang="he">בה</foreign> (<hi type="italic">bahh</hi>), <hi type="italic">in her</hi>, does not allow us to refer this to men. It is more accurately described by others to be a substantive noun; and, therefore, I have resolved to render it literally, <hi type="italic">there shall not be darkness</hi> in Judea <hi type="italic">according to the affliction of the time when, etc</hi>. Some explain <foreign xml:lang="he">הקל</foreign> (<hi type="italic">hekal</hi>) to mean that the land was <hi type="italic">relieved of a burden</hi>, in consequence of the people having been carried into captivity; but this is altogether at variance with the Prophet’s meaning, and does not agree with what follows; for it is immediately added that the seacoast has been <hi type="italic">more grievously afflicted</hi> by a second calamity. There can be no doubt, therefore, that this verb corresponds to the other verb <foreign xml:lang="he">הכביד</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">hikbid</hi>.) <note n="139"> <div sID="gen41733" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="he">הקל</foreign> (<hi type="italic">hekal</hi>) signifies literally <hi type="italic">to make light</hi>, and in accordance with an English idiom, sometimes denotes figuratively, <hi type="italic">to make light of</hi>. Stock’s rendering is, <hi type="italic">he made vile</hi>, answering to Lowth’s, <hi type="italic">he debased</hi>. Both agree in rendering <foreign xml:lang="he">הכביד</foreign> (<hi type="italic">hikbid</hi>) <hi type="italic">he hath made it glorious</hi>. The English version concurs with Calvin in rendering <foreign xml:lang="he">הקל</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">hekal</hi>,) <hi type="italic">he lightly afflicted</hi>, and <foreign xml:lang="he">הבביד</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">hikbid</hi>,) <hi type="italic">he did</hi> <hi type="italic">more grievously afflict</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen41733" type="x-p"/> </note> Not more than a small part of the kingdom having been afflicted by Tiglath-pileser, the calamity which he brought upon it is said to be light as compared with the second which was inflicted by Shalmanezer.<div eID="gen41732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41734" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">By the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the Gentiles.</hi> He calls it <hi type="italic">the way of the sea</hi>, because <hi type="italic">Galilee</hi> was adjoining to the coast of the Mediterranean <hi type="italic">Sea</hi>, and on one side it was bounded by the course of the <hi type="italic">Jordan</hi>.
